strength: Disciplined and honest. Every number checks out against my data, the projections are modest, there are ready-to-use titles and meta, and the day-60 decision rules tell the team what to do when a page doesn't move.
mistake: It pushes the cookie-banner rewrite to month 2 and values it only at the blog rate, even though it is Maya's own question with 44,000 impressions. It also never consolidates or redirects the decaying blog posts, and it does nothing specific for Tomas.
to10: Move the cookie-banner rewrite into week 1. Add a merge-and-redirect pass on the dead blog posts. Add docs-to-trial links and one page aimed at agencies or DPO questions, all still inside the 12-page limit.

strength: Wider coverage that still fits 12 pages. It does the cookie-banner rewrite in month 1 with the right nuance about other tools on a site, adds a GA4 history page for Maya and an agency/DPO page for Tomas, puts trial prompts on docs, and merges or redirects dead blog posts.
mistake: The projections lean optimistic. Taking /vs-google-analytics from position 4.2 to the top 3 for +100 trials is a ceiling dressed up as a plan. Weekly trial reporting will also be noisy, and month 3 is left fairly vague.
to10: Give a conservative-to-ceiling range for each month instead of a single ceiling. Add ready-to-use titles and meta. Replace the vague month-3 slots with clear decision rules for what gets the second pass.

strength: The work is disciplined throughout. It shows the seat math cleanly, puts a real stat beside every feature section, refuses to claim reminders cut no-shows when no figure backs it, and keeps the CTA focused on teams.
mistake: The sample-size calculation uses the 3.1% homepage-to-signup rate as the baseline for demo requests, which is a different metric, so the 13,400-visitor stop rule is shaky. Also, the security proof does not sit next to the demo form.
to10: Use Priya's 'email tennis' in the hero itself and put a security link or line right beside the final demo form. Base the stop rule on a realistic demo-request baseline or flag that assumption.

strength: The hero uses Priya's own words ('No email tennis'). Bracketed placeholders keep it honest about unknown facts. It also gives smart side moves: a security link in the top menu, an 'interviews per week' field in the form, and a metric that filters for real recruiting teams.
mistake: It adds unsupported claims: 'three or four emails' per interview, 'your week gone' at 60 interviews, and a 'Fewer missed interviews' headline with no data. The deciding metric is also a composite of two actions rather than the one clean metric I asked for.
to10: Strip the invented numbers and the no-show outcome claim, and settle on one simple deciding metric. Make the two hero variants differ more in structure, not just in angle.

strength: Front-loads the missed forecast, the margin drop and a correct 33–37 month runway range. It also adds a sharp check that direct-created databases grew only 2.6%, so nearly all growth came from the AI-builder channel.
mistake: The '9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop' aside is confusing and invites questions. It never says Customer A's exit will pull NRR down. It also runs at or slightly over the word limit.
to10: Cut the margin-math aside and state the NRR impact of Customer A. Give an expected range for the margin recovery from the 48-hour pause. Trim to clearly under 700 words.

strength: Built for the phone-reading lead partner: three numbers, bad news, and 'what we need most' all sit on the first screen. Each problem is paired with a concrete action, and the asks are dated and include a forwardable blurb that angels can actually send.
mistake: It is probably over 700 words. Burn and runway are split between the top and section 2, which makes them slightly repetitive. Like Output 1, it doesn't quantify the expected effect of the pause or Customer A's hit to NRR.
to10: Trim to under 700 words and merge the runway points. Add an expected range for margin recovery after the 48-hour pause. Note how much Customer A will pull NRR down in February.

strength: It goes straight to the right segment and trigger. The pilot math checks out: 3.1% overall, 38 of 44 positive replies booked at 86%, and the leave-out table is clean. Step 1 opens on their pricing change and the rev rec rebuild, with no link.
mistake: The 8% forecast (7–10%) rests on an invented 1.25x uplift for combining role and trigger, so the top end reads more like hope than pilot data. Step 4's 'Closing the loop' is a stock subject line.
to10: Forecast from the pilot floor, around 7%, and stop there. Leave out the pilot Controllers who already got the old sequence. Give step 4 a subject line that sounds like us.

strength: The forecast is honest: 6.8–7.9%, with an explicit refusal to multiply effects the pilot never tested together. It also adds smart list rules: rest the 1,300 Controllers already contacted and route 'later' replies to next quarter. The low-friction one-word reply asks suit busy finance people.
mistake: It promises a 'one-page summary' and 'three steps' that don't exist yet, so someone has to write them. 'Within 60 days' and 'within a few days of the flag' are used a little loosely, and the piece is close to or slightly over the 900-word limit.
to10: Write or confirm the one-page summary and the three steps before launch. Tighten the timing rule to 'within two working days of the flag.' Trim to stay safely under 900 words.

strength: The exercises feel real. The Priya invite typo gives a findable fix and a deadline, and the 03:00 login outage tests the solo-shift judgment. The time zone table, with summer hours, removes any doubt about what the hours mean where you live.
mistake: The salary sits halfway down the post, after the hard parts and requirements, not in the first screen. The post and scorecard are also dense, so they read more like a spec than a calm note.
to10: Put $82,000 right under the title. Trim the post so it breathes. Keep writing as the clearly dominant scorecard line, rather than splitting it across three rows that a reviewer has to add up.

strength: It reads the way we talk. The salary is the first line, and the weekend rotation gets its own section that says plainly why we're saying it up front. Writing carries 50% with clean 1/3/5 anchors. The review-hours math is shown, including second reads and shortlist sizes.
mistake: It gives local hours only for Singapore, Manila and Perth. Australia, NZ, Japan and summer-time shifts are left for the applicant to work out. The interview stage is also a bit vague: two video calls with no stated length.
to10: Add a short hours-by-city line that includes Sydney and Auckland. Name the longer exercise and say how long it takes. Give the conversation stage a concrete duration and the questions we'll ask.

strength: Every move has a checked, ranged projection built from our own numbers: the per-1,000 trial table, 378 to 588 extra AWT conversions and 48 to 80 Lite saves. It also correctly calls Lite the biggest leak (70% of churners).
mistake: It ranks by 'quickest money per effort' rather than by impact as I asked, which pushes the agency reporting bet to last. It also gives the data no dates, against our 'every claim has a number and a date' rule.
to10: Rank by impact, or make the case for a different ranking openly. Tie the AWT multi-site track explicitly to the agency report. Date the data sources.

strength: It joins the moves together. The agency report is the focused bet, PPC parity is explicitly refused, and the AWT multi-site track feeds into the report. It adds sharp churn facts: only 37% of Lite left after 12 months, usage limits cause a third of all churn, and Semrush is only about 2% of churn.
mistake: Move 5 (link-data studies) is close to the generic 'do more content' advice and has a weak success metric. The 'November 2026' date looks invented rather than sourced.
to10: Replace or sharpen Move 5 with a number-backed lever, such as smoothing the Lite-to-Standard price step. Give Moves 4 and 5 projected sizes. Use real source dates.

strength: Strong go/no-go gates: migration proven on 1,000 real setups, one-step undo, top 200 extensions tested, and a rule to mention only claims that are in the build. The X thread credits authors and refuses an unmeasured speed number.
mistake: The table is titled 'ranked by users who stay' but puts extension authors (2,470) above X (3,740), so the ranking contradicts its own numbers. The timeline also has no owners, and leaning on frozen engineers for support shifts is a thin capacity plan.
to10: Fix the ranking logic or state the method. Add an owner to each row. Give support a concrete staffing rota. Add measures with a plan B, and trim the X thread so each post carries one shortcut.

strength: It opens with a clear decision summary. Existing users get waves sized from the 420,000 list and gated on migration tickets. Product Hunt and HN are pushed to after the rollout. Every row has an owner, support has a staffed rota, and plan B has numeric triggers. All of it fits our real team and the 1 December code freeze.
mistake: It ranks authors above X by retention rate rather than retained count. That choice is stated, but a strict 'users who stay' reading would put X second. The email is a bit thin on showing the product moving.
to10: Show both views, retained count and retention rate, and justify putting authors ahead on growth potential. Name example author credits in the email. Add a short clip to the email body.

strength: A sharp single recommendation aimed at the Essentials 8+ leak. The per-1,000-customer churn scenarios are correct, the stop rules are clean, and the invite email is in our voice, with the customer's own price difference shown.
mistake: It talks itself out of the yearly-billing push with a shaky payback argument and ignores the 0.9% vs 4.0% churn gap. That leaves the cheapest fast win off the table, and the yearly default on the pricing page is never fixed.
to10: Add an honest yearly nudge alongside Agency, either an in-app offer or a yearly default on the page. Show a total-business net figure with the Team downgrade assumption built in, not only per-1,000 switchers.

strength: The whole-business view: the Essentials 8+ share of churned revenue, base and downside cases with Team downgrades netted out, and the break-even downgrade rate. It also tests downgrade risk directly on Team customers and offers yearly at the switch.
mistake: The customer message is a little softer and less concrete than it could be: it shows no price difference and has a slightly generic opening. The day-one net of +$2.7k is thin, and the plan doesn't flag clearly enough that most of the gain depends on an unproven churn drop.
to10: Show each customer the exact difference in the email. Add a yearly default on the pricing page as a parallel quick test. State plainly that new prices only reach new customers, so the two-quarter gain rests on retention.

strength: A full 24-post calendar with working titles for every slot, a smart rerun of an approved clip in week 4, and clear review flags on each draft.
mistake: It sends every sleep post to review, even ones that name no condition. That leaves week 1 with zero sleep posts and loses our best-performing theme for a whole week. The review rule only covers named conditions.
to10: Put condition-free wind-down posts like 'switch your brain off' in week 1 so they skip review. Use the 'can't switch my brain off' hook in a draft. Keep the full calendar.

strength: Week 1 leads with sleep and wind-down posts worded to skip review. All six drafts are in our warm voice, each ends with one small action, and they can go out on 16 November.
mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 get only weekly angles, no post titles, yet it tells me to submit them all for review on 16 November. It also keeps a weekly stress-at-work post when that slot could go to another sleep post.
to10: Add titles for every post in weeks 2 to 4 so the review batch is real. Swap the stress-at-work slot for sleep. Use 'can't switch my brain off' word for word as a hook.

strength: The series is built on the two retention habits, with clean platform branching, a calm inactivity email, and Pro moved to day 14 for engaged users only. That keeps the revenue path without spending goodwill.
mistake: The Pro email's tip depends on a paid feature, which blurs the one-tip idea. The trigger logic is looser than it should be: there is no rule for when two emails come due at once, and the second-device email is a fixed day 3 rather than tied to the user's progress.
to10: Add send-collision rules and gate email 3 on progress. Count the subject-line characters. Measure the main number by day 7 and by day 14 so the Pro email's effect is visible.

strength: The trigger logic is tight and laid out in an at-a-glance table. Email 3 fires after the recurring task or on day 4, goal actions skip emails, there is a one-email-per-24-hours rule, and each subject line shows its character count. The mobile branch is written with care for phone-first users.
mistake: Email 5 repeats email 2's ask, so the series has less range. It also drops Pro entirely and offers no plan for the upgrade revenue.
to10: Use email 5 for something new, or give it to the second-device habit for people who already have repeats. Say where the Pro ask moves after onboarding.

strength: The numbers are checked and the forecasts are cautious. Each move gets a trial range tied to a CTR assumption and the comparison-page conversion rate. Week 1 is a day-by-day list with ready titles and metas, and the day-60 rules make the plan self-correcting.
mistake: The cheap wins come late: the cookie-banner rewrite is in month 2 and the cookies page in week 4. It also doesn't plan redirecting or merging the decaying blog posts, and it adds no dedicated page for Maya's old-data worry or for Tomas. The length is probably a little over 1,000 words.
to10: Put the cookie-banner post and the cookies-page retitle in the first two weeks, since they are quick wins on pages already near page one. Add a merge or redirect step for the decaying blog posts. Add a dedicated GA4 migration page. Trim to the word limit.

strength: The range of ideas is wider and aimed at both buyers. It adds a GA4 history migration page for Maya, an agency page for Tomas, a /compare hub, and a stop item to merge or redirect dead posts. Each month is laid out with writer and developer tasks.
mistake: The forecast is inflated. It assumes /vs-google-analytics reaches a 9% CTR, which is the branded /vs-matomo rate and is unrealistic for a generic query. The result is +100 trials from one page and a 175-trial, 67-customer ceiling, partly built on a speculative docs-prompt guess. Developer-day loads also look like more than one day's work.
to10: Use realistic CTR targets, and drop or clearly flag the guessed docs-prompt gain. Make the developer days fit one day each. Put the cookie-banner post and cookies page first in week 1, and give ready titles and metas. Cut the unconfirmed migration and agency pages, or tie them to confirmed facts and capacity.

strength: Disciplined and honest: the seat math is shown, the assumptions are stated up front (no PTO or hiring-tool claims beyond what is known), and the test has a single clean metric (demo requests per visitor) with a worked sample-size stop rule. Copy is ready to paste.
mistake: Section 3 says 'If PTO is on someone's calendar, they're skipped' right after the assumptions say it claims no PTO feature beyond calendar availability. That is a small inconsistency. Hero A's 71% proof line is also a first-booking-within-7-days figure from signups, which could be read as a claim about teams, not recruiting visitors. It stays at the 1,000-word limit, though the total looks close to or slightly over it.
to10: Use Priya's own phrase 'email tennis' in the hero, make the security proof visible near the first demo button instead of only in section 6, and make the PTO wording consistent with the stated assumption.

strength: The hero uses Priya's own words ('No email tennis') and names round robin that skips anyone who is off. The bracketed placeholders for unknown facts (security, logos, quote) avoid inventing proof, and the metric ties to real recruiting use.
mistake: The metric 'qualified team starts' mixes demo bookings with signups plus a first booking within 7 days. That is a blended, harder-to-measure number rather than one clean metric. The stop rule is vague ('at least two full weeks', '95% confidence') with no sample size. Mixing 'Get started' and 'Book a demo' on a team page muddies the single action. Section 2 states 'three or four emails' and '60 interviews a week' as if they were facts, and 'Candidates can reschedule from the same link' and 'email or text reminders' are unsupported feature claims. It also has nine sections, which adds length.
to10: Use one deciding metric with a sample-size rule, keep the demo button consistent on a team page, check or flag the text-reminder and reschedule claims, and put a security cue near the hero button.

strength: The top is built for a phone reader: three numbers, then a numbered bad-news list, then the headline ask with a date. The math checks out, including the roughly 476,000 AI-builder share of the 500,000 database increase, and the forwardable blurb for the VP ask is useful.
mistake: It is clearly over the 700-word limit. It repeats the bad news in a list and again in a long section. The angel ask for free-tier advice is soft, and the New York base is a plan rather than a decision with a date.
to10: Cut it to 700 words by merging the bad-news list with the explanations. Add a one-line expected effect of the 48-hour pause on margin. Say Customer A will pull NRR down. Make the angel ask sharper and commit to a decision on the New York base.

strength: It ties the margin drop to the AI-builder channel with real analysis. $0.9M on about $10.4M of monthly revenue is roughly 9 points of margin, which more than explains the 7-point drop. It also shows direct-created databases grew only 2.6%, so nearly all the growth came from the channel, and it gives a 33 to 37 month runway range.
mistake: It uses two tables when the brief asked for a small one, and it is still near or slightly over 700 words. It states opening the New York base as a plan even though its own assumptions say that needs confirming. The 'Ask 2 helps' line is awkward.
to10: Trim a little to land under 700 words. Fold the burn table into one line or the main table. Note that Customer A will pull NRR down. Confirm the New York decision and the ask dates, and tighten the margin math caveat.

strength: Exactly follows the pilot: Controllers only, pricing-change trigger, no links in any email, and a clean load/leave-out table with an honest per-100 projection and visible working.
mistake: The 10% ceiling (7.9% x 1.25) is an invented multiplier, and the 8% headline sits above what the pilot supports. Step 1 also carries the proof, but it is a plain-text sentence, so that is fine. The Step 4 'nine days and three spreadsheets' echo is slightly gimmicky.
to10: Anchor the expectation at the pilot-backed 7% with no invented uplift. Add a short line on how the rep writes the {{change}} field. Make each ask more concrete, and keep the step 3 ask on the question about who else has a say.

strength: Conservative, honest expectation (7%, floor 6.8%, no multiplying untested gains) and a thoughtful exclusion list that includes the pilot Controllers who already got the old sequence.
mistake: Emails break the one-question, one-ask rule: step 1 asks how many days the close takes and then offers a 'reply yes' one-page summary. Step 2 has a question plus a 'reply steps' ask, and Step 3 and Step 4 do the same. It also promises a one-page summary and 'three steps' that do not exist. 'Controllers tell me' implies conversations that did not happen. The '4,100 stay out' figure is wrong, and the '130 replies, 65 positive, 55 meetings' arithmetic does not reconcile.
to10: Cut every email to one question and one ask. Remove promises of assets that do not exist. Fix the exclusion count and the rollout math, and avoid implying prior conversations.

strength: The scorecard is concrete and weights writing at 85%, backed by the 0.62 vs 0.04 data. The Priya exercise has a real typo to catch, and the shortlist exercise, call questions and a calibrated blind-read process are all included.
mistake: It runs over the 1,100-word limit, and the $82,000 salary sits well down the post instead of on the first screen. The timezone table is also fiddly with its summer-time brackets.
to10: Cut about 150 words, move the salary to the top line, and simplify the timezone table. Keep the typo-based exercise and the 1/3/5 rows.

strength: The post is calm and candid. It opens with the salary, names the overnight gap honestly, gives the weekend rotation its own section and keeps within a tight length.
mistake: The scorecard is thinner. Its 1/3/5 descriptions are generic, there is no sample shortlist exercise or call questions, and the 'why this job?' prompt reintroduces a mini cover letter.
to10: Add a concrete longer exercise and the call questions. Make the 1/3/5 examples specific to the reply (for example, what a 5 does with the invoice deadline). Drop or justify the 'why this job' question.

strength: Pairs a clear 'where we lose' diagnosis (agencies 27% of trials but 60% of Semrush losses) with five owned, testable moves, including holdout tests, and an explicit 'what not to do' section.
mistake: Ranks agency reporting first although it is the longest build, while the Lite usage-limit fix, the fastest money, is second. Move 5 (content) is weak, with no number and a vague first step. The 'about 2% of churn' figure and the 12-month 37% survival are extra derivations that may be off.
to10: Put the Lite limit fix first as the fastest money, with reporting as the focused bigger bet. Replace move 5 with something quantified. Tighten the claims about unsourced derived numbers and state a clear date source.

strength: Ranks by speed to money with an explicit rule. It leads with the multi-site Webmaster Tools track and the Lite top-up, and puts reporting last as the longest build. Every move carries a named assumption and a projected range, and it uses 'Here's the data.'
mistake: Ranking agency reporting last, even with the caveat, may undersell the strategic bet. It has only four moves, so less range, and the projections rest on assumed lifts. 'About 9 customers per 10,000' for Semrush churn is a bit opaque.
to10: Clarify how the multi-site track and the reporting build connect, and explain why reporting comes last despite being the main competitive gap. Add a short note on the 'nurture to trial' mechanic and show the derivation of the 9 per 10,000 figure.

strength: Ranks channels with the math, sets eight pre-launch gates (migration test, undo, support, staged rollout), and gives a full dated timeline with a five-post X thread and a warm email. Product Hunt is moved to its own day, and the plan includes 'Start with five' for newcomers.
mistake: The channel table is not actually sorted by retained users: X (3,740) and Product Hunt (3,420) sit below authors (2,470) and Hacker News (2,940). Rank 5 for Product Hunt is also not consistent with its 3,420 retained users, which exceed Hacker News and authors. The plan also launches Show HN on day one, and engineers are asked to work support shifts. The X post names an AI command builder with a made-up example as shipped, and the speed placeholder has stripped values.
to10: State plainly that the ranking is by retention rate, or by retained users, and stay consistent. Keep the speed claim out of the post until measured. Add owners per task, and state the wave-size math (how many users in each rollout step). Tighten to the word limit.

strength: Opens with the decision, then makes a sharp call: stage the rollout in waves gated by migration ticket share, move Product Hunt and Hacker News to 15 December after the rollout is done, and secure a freeze exception for migration hotfixes. It sets measurable targets, a day-4 check with plan B, a no-go rule that still lets new installs go, and a support rota with owners on each row.
mistake: Some numbers are shaky: 'YouTube and authors brought 19% of installs but 41% of users who stayed' is roughly right (17,500 of 93,500 is 19%, and 6,980 of 17,080 is 41%), but 'the share kit and creators with 9 videos' projection of 16,500 installs assumes linear scaling. The 10-second author clip in a Monday 30 Nov kit is also tight. The email says 'carried over' in the past tense before the rollout is confirmed, and the X post is thinner than the other plan's thread.
to10: Hedge the projection more clearly, and add a longer X thread with a different shortcut per post. Phrase the email so it matches what each user has actually received, and keep to 1,200 words.

strength: The 8+ segment is sized correctly and the revenue math checks out per 1,000 switchers, at three churn levels including the 4.1% case I hoped to see. The customer messages are in our voice and include the invite email, a pricing page card and a public post. Each says plainly that nothing changes for current prices.
mistake: The first test invites only Essentials 8+ customers, so the Team downgrade risk it names is never measured before launch. It is only caught by a rule after launch. The math is also per 1,000 switchers, with no company-level view the board can read against two quarters.
to10: Include Team 8+ customers in the test so cannibalization is measured. Show net company revenue at month 6 with a downside case. Offer yearly billing at the switch as a cheap, honest push, not just as a later test. Drop the awkward 'bad news first' line.

strength: The math is built up to a net company figure: +$2.7k on day one and +$23k a month by month 6, after Team downgrades. It adds a downside case and a break-even, which is that the plan loses money if more than about 1 in 3 Team 8+ customers move down. The test invites Team 8+ customers too, with clear go and stop thresholds on switch rate, churn and downgrades.
mistake: The 5% churn for switchers and the 50% switch rate are assumed, not grounded, and the model is a bit dense. The customer copy is thinner than it should be: it has no pricing page text, and the email uses a placeholder for the current bill. Yearly billing appears only as a line inside the switch offer.
to10: Add pricing page copy and a launch post draft. Offer yearly billing to existing monthly customers on its own, as the fastest win. Show why the 5% churn assumption is reasonable, and simplify the revenue table for the team.

strength: Puts sleep and narrator clips at the center, with night posting, a stop list, and a measurable success test. The warm drafts use the customer's own hook.
mistake: Sends every sleep post to review, so week 1 has no sleep posts and is all kindness. Three of the six drafts are week 1 kindness posts. The week 1 and calendar logic is muddled: it says Tuesday 24 November but week 1 slots have drafts labeled sleep in the table. The projection also has errors, such as a 4,300 target against a 7,650 projection, and the calendar shows week 1 as kindness while the pattern table says sleep. Draft 5 has a 'put your phone across the room' instruction that edges toward 'you should' language.
to10: Fill week 1 with non-reviewed winding-down posts in the evening rather than all kindness. Keep the calendar consistent with the pattern table. Make the drafts match the plan, and give clear dates for submitting reviewed posts.

strength: Week 1 is sleep-led and evening-timed, and its 6 drafts are written to avoid naming any condition, so they need no review. They use 'replaying emails' and 'busy mind' hooks, with the clear plan to submit weeks 2 to 4 on 16 November. The drafts are ready to hand to the team.
mistake: Keeps 4 stress-at-work posts and a daytime parent slot. Its claim that week 1 needs no review is a judgment call, since busy-mind-at-night content could be argued to touch sleep conditions. It also leaves a loose end in the assumed reviewed-post timing, and the calendar for weeks 2 to 4 is not spelled out.
to10: Shift the mix further to sleep by dropping the stress-at-work posts and giving a week-by-week table for weeks 2 to 4. Flag clearly that the sleep drafts avoid naming conditions, and explain why they skip review.

strength: Tight trigger and skip logic: emails fire off the allowed events, skip when the goal is already met, and a 24-hour cap prevents pile-ups. The platform-branched second-device email is strong.
mistake: Email 5 repeats email 2's recurring-task ask, so the series has little range. It also removes Pro from onboarding altogether, leaving no upgrade path. A stray note to the team sits inside email 3B.
to10: Replace the repeated recurring-task email with a different tip or a gated Pro step. Put a goal and success measure under each email. Remove the internal notes from the copy.

strength: Each email has its own trigger, skip rule, goal and a "worked if" measure tied to the 14%, 22%, 8% and 31% baselines. The series builds on the two habits, branches the second-device email by platform, and keeps a calm, guilt-free inactivity email.
mistake: Email 5 is a Pro upsell, which I didn't ask for. The 0.4% unsubscribe guardrail also conflicts with beating the Pro email's 1.1% benchmark. Email 1 isn't branched by platform.
to10: Make the unsubscribe guardrail consistent with the Pro email, or drop the Pro email for a second habit-based tip. State the 1-to-4-task segment and a mobile-first welcome tweak. Note how a user with neither habit by day 14 is handled.

strength: It covers the full picture of our business. It moves capacity to comparison pages and adds a GA4 migration page for Maya and an agency page for Tomas. It also puts trial prompts on the docs pages and has a clear stop list with consolidation of dead posts.
mistake: The forecast is too rosy. It assumes /vs-google-analytics jumps to a 9% top-3 CTR, which gives a ceiling of about 175 extra trials a month that I would struggle to believe or defend. The cookie-banner rewrite also comes fourth, not first.
to10: Use more cautious forecasts given as ranges, start week 1 with the cookie-banner and cookie-free retitles, and supply ready-to-use titles and metas.

strength: The forecasts are honest ranges that I can check, and the arithmetic holds up (+41 to +95 trials, 16 to 36 paid). It gives ready-to-use titles and metas in our voice, a daily week-1 list with 'done when' checks, and day-60 rules for what to do if pages don't move.
mistake: There is no GA4 migration page or agency page, and no docs-to-trial linking. The persona worries are folded into comparison pages instead. The cookie-banner post is pushed to month 2 even though it is our biggest near-page-one opportunity.
to10: Bring the cookie-banner rewrite into month 1, add trial links from the high-CTR docs pages, and include one page aimed at Tomas's DPO and multi-site needs.

strength: It picks recruiting with the right seat math and builds the hero on Priya's own 'email tennis' pain. It also moves routing and security up the page and cuts the demo form to 4 fields.
mistake: Buttons switch between 'Get started' and 'Book a demo' on a page for teams. It also invents a '3–4 emails per interview, your week gone' claim, and the deciding metric is a compound one that waits 7 days for a first booking.
to10: Use one consistent team call to action and drop the made-up email count. Pick a simpler deciding metric with a sample-size rule, and put the security proof right next to the final demo button.

strength: It is careful and ready to ship. It states what it assumes about the product (calendar-based PTO skipping, no ATS integration claimed), keeps every button on 'Book a demo', uses real numbers as proof (71%, 41%, 88%, 74%), and names a clean deciding metric with a stop rule.
mistake: The sample-size math uses the 3.1% homepage signup rate as the baseline for demo requests, so the visitor target is likely far too low. The two hero versions are also a bit close in wording.
to10: Base the test sizing on the real demo-request rate and put Priya's 'email tennis' phrase in the hero. Make Version B a clearer outcome-led idea.

strength: It explains the margin drop well. The $0.9M of extra compute on about $10.4M of monthly revenue is roughly 9 points of margin, and direct-created databases grew only 2.6%, so nearly all the growth came from a channel that rarely pays.
mistake: The fix for the AI app builders stops at the 48-hour pause. It does not change how we judge those partners, and it never says what the pause should save, even as a range. The markdown headers may also not display properly in an email client.
to10: Give an expected range for the margin recovery after the 48-hour pause. Add a forwardable blurb for the VP Enterprise Sales intros. Format it as plain email text.

strength: The phone-reading lead partner gets everything in the first screen: the three numbers, the missed forecast, the bad news and the top ask with a date. The forwardable VP blurb makes the angels' intros easy, and adding a runway row to the table is useful.
mistake: It is long and may run past the 700-word limit. Like the other draft, it gives no expected range for the margin recovery from the 48-hour pause.
to10: Trim it to fit within 700 words and add an expected effect of the pause on gross margin, given as a range.

strength: The reply-rate forecast is honest. It is anchored at 6.8% to 7.9% from the pilot and refuses to multiply two effects the pilot never tested together. It also spots that the 1,300 pilot Controllers who already got the old sequence need a rest period.
mistake: Some lines are clunky. Step 4's 'the 9 to 4 day close I shared is the reason I wrote' reads awkwardly. Step 3's subject assumes they have an audit coming.
to10: Tighten the step 4 wording and make the step 3 subject neutral. Show the pilot-wide baseline next to the projection so I can see the lift at a glance.

strength: The presentation is very clear. The 'who, when, how' summary and the leave-out table are easy to follow. The comparison against the pilot-wide baseline (3.1%, 1.4%, 1.2%) is calculated correctly, and step 3 usefully brings engineering into the conversation.
mistake: The 8% forecast with a 10% ceiling rests on a made-up 1.25 multiplier, and the 7% floor sits above what this segment actually did (6.8%). It also never says to hold back the pilot Controllers who were already contacted.
to10: Ground the forecast in the pilot numbers alone and drop the invented multiplier. Exclude contacts from the earlier sequence. Replace the stock subject 'Closing the loop'.

strength: Puts the salary first and states the hours and weekend rotation plainly. It also does the reviewer-hours maths (70 hours against 160) with a sensible second-read step, so I can trust the application plan.
mistake: The longer written exercise and the video-call questions are only mentioned, never written. The hiring team would still have to build them before using the scorecard.
to10: Write out the shortlist exercise and the call questions. Make the application reply test a fixable problem as well as tone, so it can feed the problem-solving score too.

strength: Very concrete. The Priya reply hides a fixable typo, so one short task tests both writing and problem-solving. It also gives a local-hours table for each city, a fully written shortlist exercise, fixed call questions, and a scorecard tied to each exercise.
mistake: The salary sits halfway down the post instead of in the first screen. The 'summer' brackets in the hours table could confuse people, because southern and northern summers fall at different times of year.
to10: Move the $82,000 to the top. Label the daylight-saving columns by month instead of 'summer'. Add a decision rule (minimum total score, no line below 3).

strength: Every move has a sized projection with a named assumption, and the numbers check out: Lite is 70% of churners, the multi-site free accounts bring 42% of free-tier conversions, and Advanced customers leaving for Semrush are only about 9 per 10,000 a month.
mistake: I asked for moves ranked by impact, but it ranks them by quickest money and puts the agency report last. That undersells the one place Semrush actually beats us. It also never puts a date on the data, and our voice says every claim has a number and a date.
to10: Rank by impact as asked, or argue the order more strongly. Date the data. Tie the multi-site free-account onboarding track directly to the agency report so the two moves work together.

strength: It makes the agency report the focused bet and refuses PPC parity. It links the multi-site free-account track to that report and calls Lite our biggest leak, backed by sharp numbers: 37% of Lite customers remain after a year, and usage limits cause about a third of all churn. It also says plainly what not to do, including cutting prices for creators.
mistake: Move 5, the content studies, is the generic 'do more content' idea with a thin success measure and no projection. The enterprise move also has no sized projection, unlike the others.
to10: Replace or sharpen Move 5, add a projection for the enterprise pack, and say why Lite sits second rather than first even though it is the cheapest, fastest money.

strength: It ties every decision to our numbers. Existing users get the update in three waves, and each wave goes out only if migration tickets stay low. Product Hunt and Hacker News move to after the rollout. There is a dated timeline with owners, a go/no-go checklist, and a day-4 plan B.
mistake: It leans hard on a tiny team: the launch manager also answers tickets on wave days. The email's subject line ('Your hotkeys didn't move') makes a firm promise before the beta has proven it. The email thanks the community but names no extension authors.
to10: Name specific authors in the email. Pull engineers in to cover support during the freeze instead of the launch manager. Soften the hotkey promise until the 300-tester gate passes. Add a short newcomer message (where to start) for the product manager and designer group.

strength: It has good audience-specific ideas: 'Start with five' for newcomers with authors credited, engineers joining support during the freeze, and a strict claims gate that drops any feature or speed number not in the build. It also covers more channels and messages.
mistake: The timeline is too tight and does not hang together. The 1,000-user beta starts 23 Nov, only a week before the freeze, and creators get builds on 24 Nov. The plan says existing users get the update in stages, yet emails all 420,000 on day one and tells them how to update now. Hacker News launches on the same day, and the timeline has no owners. Post 2 has a broken placeholder.
to10: Move the beta and creator builds earlier, before 20 Nov. Add owners to the timeline. Send the email in step with each update wave. Remove the 'update now' line and the broken speed placeholder. Cut the X thread down to one shortcut.

strength: It aims squarely at the Essentials 8+ leak and backs that with a base case and a downside case. It also builds the biggest risk, Team customers moving down, into the test: it invites a random 20% of Team 8+ customers and sets a clear stop threshold.
mistake: The month-6 revenue table is hard to follow; I couldn't easily trace how $41.7k was reached. The yearly-billing push only appears as an offer at the moment of switching. It doesn't fix the default-to-monthly toggle on the pricing page.
to10: Show the churn-saving math step by step. Add a cheap fix for yearly billing: show yearly by default, or offer it in-app after 60 days. That is the fastest win inside the board's two quarters.

strength: The per-1,000-switcher math is very clear, with three churn cases I can check myself. The customer messaging is complete and in our voice: invite email, pricing page card and public post. It is honest that 14+ channel accounts will pay less.
mistake: It dismisses the yearly-billing push with a shaky payback argument and leaves the default-to-monthly problem untouched. It also only watches Team downgrades after public launch rather than in the test.
to10: Test Team downgrade risk before launch. Treat yearly default or an in-app yearly offer as a parallel quick win instead of arguing it away.

strength: It puts sleep wind-down posts in week 1 and words them so they skip review, so our best install driver starts on day one, in the evening, with narrator clips.
mistake: Weeks 2 to 4 are only a repeated weekly slot plus one-line angles, with no post-by-post calendar. It also keeps a weekly stress-at-work slot, which tilts the mix less toward sleep than the data supports.
to10: Add a full 24-post calendar with titles for weeks 2 to 4 and a review flag on each post. Give more of the weekly slots to sleep, and use our 'Take a breath. You've got this.' line.

strength: It gives a complete 24-post calendar, flags review for each draft, and sets a clear submission schedule that covers Thanksgiving. It also reuses an already-approved clip in week 4, and the projections are correct.
mistake: It sends every sleep post to review, so week 1 has no sleep posts at all. Careful wording could have avoided review and given us a full week of our best-performing theme.
to10: Write wind-down posts for week 1 that name no condition and so skip review. Also tidy a few instructional lines, such as 'After you save this'.

strength: A tight design built on the two habits that predict retention. It branches by signup platform, uses only the triggers our tool supports, and the at-a-glance table and drop table both carry the right numbers.
mistake: It drops the Pro email entirely and gives no plan for revenue. Email 5 also repeats email 2's recurring-task ask instead of adding something new.
to10: Replace the redundant email 5 with a carefully targeted Pro email or another habit step. Measure both habits within the same 7-day window as today's 8% baseline.

strength: Each email has its own goal and success measure, as I asked. It branches by platform, sets skip rules, and makes the both-habits rate in week one the main number. Pro moves to day 14, only for engaged users, with a 0.4% unsubscribe guardrail.
mistake: The Pro email mixes an upgrade pitch with a tip, so it doesn't fully keep the one-tip rule. It also states a Pro feature claim that should be checked. The welcome email slips in a second tip about date parsing, and a one-month holdout is tight for reading day-30 retention.
to10: Make the Pro email a single clean ask. Check the reminder claim. Run the holdout long enough to measure day-30 retention properly.

strength: The numbers are right and the forecasts are cautious, with ranges tied to our own CTRs and the 38% trial-to-paid rate. The Monday-to-Friday week-1 plan and the ready-to-use titles and meta lines are in our voice, with no fear copy and no GDPR guarantee.
mistake: The 2022 cookie-banner post is ranked last and held to month 2, though it is a cheap win on Maya's exact phrase. There is also no plan to merge or redirect the decaying blog posts, and no page built for Tomas.
to10: Do the cookie-banner rewrite in the first month. Add a merge or redirect step for the dead blog posts, and a page or section aimed at the agency buyer. Trim it to the 1,000-word limit.

strength: It has the widest range of ideas that fit our buyers: a GA4 migration page for Maya, an agency page for Tomas, a compare hub, and a merge or redirect of dead posts. The honest note that other tools on a site may still need a cookie banner is good.
mistake: The forecast is too optimistic: +100 trials from one rewrite and about +25 from an unproven docs prompt, giving a 175-trial ceiling. The developer-day tasks also look like more than one day a month, and the plan asks the owner for a facts check when I'm not available.
to10: Use cautious ranges and a realistic developer load. Put the cookie-banner rewrite in week 1 and write the actual titles and meta. Cut the 'send to owner' step and keep it within the word limit.

strength: It is tightly tied to our numbers and ranks work by trial impact, not traffic. The projections are mostly careful and the plan fits the 12-page and 3-dev-day constraint.
mistake: It starts with the GA comparison rewrite and pushes the cookie-banner/no-cookies cheap wins slightly later than I would like. It also claims every alternative page will have a check date, but the page schedule does not quite cover all of them.
to10: Move the cookie-banner rewrite and the 'website analytics without cookies' retitle into week one or month one, and make the comparison refresh list exact so all nine pages are accounted for.

strength: It reads like a practical operating plan and gets the main strategic call right: stop feeding the general blog and put writer time into comparison and buyer-intent pages.
mistake: The forecast is too optimistic, especially assuming /vs-google-analytics can reach a 9% CTR and calling the full upside a likely ceiling. It also adds pages that are less clearly backed by the search data, and asks for owner/product confirmation despite the brief saying the owner is not available.
to10: Tighten the forecast ranges, schedule the no-cookies page earlier, remove unsupported product claims, and replace the owner check with a self-contained fact-check step using public sources.

strength: It picks recruiting for the right reason, shows the paid-seat math clearly, and builds the page around the real buyer pain: candidate email tennis, round robin, routing, and security.
mistake: It slightly over-specifies testing math and makes a couple of assumptions about PTO/calendar behavior that would need checking before publishing.
to10: Remove the slightly awkward assumptions about the homepage staying as-is, verify the PTO/calendar wording, and make the security/demo proof exactly match what is live today.

strength: It understands the segment and the main conversion path, and the deciding metric is smart because it rewards qualified recruiting team usage, not empty clicks.
mistake: It adds some unproven claims or specifics, like three or four emails, text reminders, rescheduling behavior, video tools, and people being off, and it uses Get started too often on a team page.
to10: Tighten the claims to only what the data supports, use Book a demo consistently for the recruiting team path, and replace bracketed placeholders with verified proof.

strength: It gets the real story right: AI-builder growth is not quality growth, it is hurting margin, and Customer A plus the missed ARR forecast are put up front.
mistake: It is a little over-drafted for a finished investor email: two tables plus an assumptions section make it feel like a draft, and the margin-point explanation is useful but slightly more analytical than I would want in the sent version.
to10: Tighten the email by cutting the assumptions section or moving it into cleaner footnotes, keep one compact metric table, and make the Customer A action more specific with an owner and date.

strength: It is very close to sendable: clear first screen, correct numbers, bad news early, and the asks are specific with owners and dates.
mistake: It is slightly less sharp on the core insight: it says AI app builders hurt margin, but does not quantify as clearly how much of the database growth is low-quality or how the $0.9M compute increase explains the margin drop.
to10: Add the direct-vs-AI database growth math and make the 48-hour pause sound like a committed action rather than something we 'plan' to do.

strength: It follows the pilot signals closely: right persona, pricing-change timing, no links, clear exclusions, and a grounded reply-rate expectation.
mistake: The CTAs are a little over-engineered with reply words like “yes” and “steps,” and step 1 asks both for their close length and a reply trigger.
to10: Make the CTAs feel more like a finance peer and less like a sales sequence, and tighten each email to one clean question or ask.

strength: The emails sound the most natural: plain, specific, and close to how a finance person would describe the pricing-change and rev rec problem.
mistake: The 7% to 10% reply-rate range is a bit aggressive; the pilot supports about 7% to 8% more cleanly than a 10% ceiling.
to10: Use a more conservative expected reply rate, keep the projection closer to the measured 6.8% and 7.9%, and make the step 2 meeting ask slightly softer.

strength: It acts on the main signals in the data: hire for the UTC overnight gap, make the weekend rotation impossible to miss, drop experience requirements, and put a short written customer reply in the application.
mistake: The time-zone table is a little fussy and has some daylight-time confusion; I would simplify it before publishing.
to10: Tighten the published post slightly, simplify the hours examples, and make sure the 4-day summer schedule is clear for this shift.

strength: The post sounds right: direct, calm, honest about salary, hours, weekend rotation, and the hard parts.
mistake: The application writing prompt does not give the applicant enough facts to solve a real problem, so it mainly tests tone rather than the strongest signal we have: written problem-solving.
to10: Use a more concrete customer exercise with hidden facts to find and fix, specify the longer written exercise, and reduce the two video conversations unless there is a clear reason for both.

strength: It finds the real pattern: Semrush is mainly an agency/reporting/PPC problem, while our bigger leak is Lite limits and pricing friction. The math is mostly checked and useful.
mistake: It ranks the agency reporting build above the Lite limits fix, even though the Lite fix is probably the fastest money and cheaper to test. The fifth move on content is also weaker than the first four.
to10: Put the Lite usage-limit/top-up test first or make the ranking logic clearer, tighten the fifth move into something more measurable, and avoid inventing a precise data date unless it is actually in the source.

strength: Very sharp quant work. The per-1,000 trial view, AWT conversion math, and Advanced-to-Semrush churn math make the scale of each problem easy to see.
mistake: The ranking is off for this brief. It puts the reporting product bet last and the AWT email track first, even though the core competitive loss is agencies needing sendable client reports.
to10: Re-rank by business impact, not speed per unit of effort: Lite limits and agency reporting should lead. Tie the AWT nurture directly to the reporting offer once that exists or is in beta.

strength: It acts on the real signal in the data: protect migration first, put creators and extension authors ahead of Product Hunt, and stage the rollout so support does not get crushed again.
mistake: The channel table says it is ranked by week-4 share rather than retained users, which could confuse the decision even though the actual launch order is right for us.
to10: Tighten the retained-user ranking language, confirm the staged rollout mechanics, and move the final migration go/no-go earlier than the code freeze or split it into pre-freeze and launch gates.

strength: It catches the main lesson from the last launch: hotkeys and settings are the launch risk, while creators and extension authors are the highest-quality acquisition channels.
mistake: It creates avoidable launch-day load by emailing 420,000 users and posting to Show HN on day one while also claiming a staged rollout; it also assumes engineers can join support during freeze.
to10: Separate existing-user waves from broad launch noise, push HN/Product Hunt later, remove placeholders, and make the support and beta-testing plan fit the small team more realistically.

strength: It finds the real leak, gives one clear plan, shows the revenue and downgrade risk, and tests Team cannibalization before a full launch.
mistake: It underplays the broader yearly-billing opportunity; the yearly push is only attached to the new plan rather than being a larger near-term retention lever.
to10: Add a simple honest yearly-billing follow-up for existing monthly customers, tighten the churn measurement window, and make the Agency guardrails even clearer so Team is protected.

strength: The per-1,000-customer revenue math is very clear and useful, and the customer messaging sounds transparent and Buffer-like.
mistake: It does not test Team downgrades before launch, even though cannibalizing Team is the main financial risk; it also dismisses yearly billing too quickly.
to10: Include Team 8+ customers in the test before public launch, add a clear yearly-billing nudge, and clean up the month-6 math labels so every number is unambiguous.

strength: It follows the strongest commercial signal: more sleep content, more narrator clips, more evening posting, with clear stop/do guidance and usable drafts in our voice.
mistake: It is too conservative on review, treating all sleep posts as blocked until 24 November and filling week 1 with kindness, when we could run winding-down posts that avoid condition language.
to10: Use no-review week 1 wind-down/sleep-adjacent posts, correct the review timing to allow approved posts from Monday 23 November, and make the weekly calendar a little more specific by date and asset.

strength: It is clean, easy to use, gets the key numbers right, and has strong week 1 drafts built around real customer language like replaying emails and school pickup.
mistake: The review plan and calendar do not quite line up: the same weekly pattern puts a reviewed sleep post on Monday 23, while the copy says approved posts can only go live from Tuesday 24.
to10: Turn the repeated weekly pattern into a dated 4-week calendar, push the mix a bit harder toward sleep narrator clips, and clearly mark which posts need review and when each can go live.

strength: It correctly builds the whole series around the two retention signals: recurring tasks and a second device, with platform-specific second-device emails and a gentle inactivity nudge.
mistake: The Pro email is probably still a little early and introduces a paid-feature pitch that is less central than the two core habits.
to10: Tighten the Pro decision, maybe make email 5 a habit reinforcement or only test Pro after both habits are complete, and make the skip/segment rules fully explicit for every email.

strength: It focuses on the right behaviors, uses the available triggers, branches by platform, and drops the weak current emails for the right reasons.
mistake: The fifth email repeats the recurring-task ask rather than adding much new, and the main success metric shifts to day 14 instead of pushing the key week-one habit strongly enough.
to10: Make the fifth email more strategic, clean up the measurement plan around day-7 recurring plus second-device completion, and remove small overstatements like the Pro email being one lost subscriber per click.

strength: It stays tightly anchored to the actual numbers, moves capacity toward comparison pages, and gives a concrete first week the writer can start on Monday.
mistake: It says the first move should be /vs-google-analytics, but the cheaper near-page-one refreshes on the cookie-banner and no-cookies queries were the clearest quick wins from the data.
to10: Start week 1 with the cookie-banner post and the 'website analytics without cookies' page alongside the GA comparison work, and keep the same quantified forecasting and stop list.

strength: It adds useful buyer-blocker ideas like migration-history and agency/DPO messaging, and it keeps the writing plain and mostly on-brand.
mistake: It breaks focus and capacity discipline by adding net-new pages not supported by the search data, and it overstates some forecasts, especially the +100 trials for the GA page rewrite.
to10: Cut the speculative new pages, center the plan on the proven comparison and near-page-one opportunities, and tighten the math so every projected gain clearly follows from the query and conversion data.

strength: It picks the right segment with the right seat math and structures the page around the real recruiting job to be done: ending email back and forth, fair round robin, routing, then security.
mistake: It states round robin 'skips anyone who is busy or off' and mentions PTO a bit too directly without clearly limiting that to what the connected calendar shows, so it edges toward a product claim that may overreach.
to10: Tighten any risky product claims, keep one CTA path a bit more consistent for a team page, and replace placeholders with real security proof and one real recruiting quote.

strength: It reads like someone understood both the business and the buyer: it chooses recruiting for the right economic reason, uses Priya's pain in the hero, moves security up, and is careful not to invent claims.
mistake: It says the homepage hero stays as it is, even though the brief asked for the hero for a version of the page aimed at this segment; that assumption is a bit off, and the traffic math for the test is more detailed than the owner asked for.
to10: Make the assumption align exactly with the brief, trim a little of the testing math, and add the final proof assets so it is fully publishable.

strength: It reads like our company: candid, specific, numbers first, bad news up top, and the asks are concrete and useful.
mistake: It overreaches a little on the margin math and includes an assumptions section that I would likely cut before sending.
to10: Tighten the wording, remove the assumptions note from the body, and be a bit more careful where it infers causality or expected savings beyond what the data supports.

strength: It is clean, easy to scan on a phone, and does a good job of connecting the AI-builder channel to the margin problem with a practical fix.
mistake: The runway table is wrong for September, which makes me question the numbers, and that is fatal in an investor update.
to10: Fix the factual error, tighten the asks a bit, and make the most important bad news feel even more immediate by leading more clearly with Customer A and the forecast miss.

strength: It aims tightly at the right segment and trigger, uses the pilot data correctly, and gives practical list rules and realistic expected results I could actually run with.
mistake: A few emails have slightly more than one ask or feel a bit process-heavy, and step 1 asks for a reply plus offers to send a summary rather than keeping the CTA as simple as possible.
to10: Tighten each email to one cleaner ask, make step 2 and step 4 slightly sharper in finance voice, and keep the sequence even more focused on the pricing-change to close-time chain.

strength: It identifies the right segment, trigger, and no-link approach, and the structure is easy to read and operationalize.
mistake: It overreaches on projected performance and breaks the brief in places: step 2 asks for a 20-minute meeting directly, several emails do not follow the one-question-one-ask rule cleanly, and some forecast math is too speculative.
to10: Bring the expected reply rate back to the pilot-based range, simplify the CTAs to one low-friction ask per email, and revise the copy to sound more like a finance peer than a sales rep pushing a meeting.

strength: It uses our actual signals well: writing is weighted highest, the overnight UTC gap becomes the role design, and the weekend rotation is stated plainly near the top.
mistake: It changes the role title to Customer Support Specialist when the brief asked for a recruitment marketing specialist, and the sample hours table includes US Pacific even though the stated shift is 00:00 to 08:00 UTC.
to10: Keep the same data-led structure but fix the role/title mismatch and tighten the geography-hours examples so every detail lines up perfectly.

strength: It clearly explains why the application should center on a short writing task and it welcomes career changers instead of filtering for support pedigree.
mistake: It invents a different customer prompt and adds a 'why this job' question, which pulls us back toward motivational screening instead of sticking to the strongest signal in our data.
to10: Use the exact operational problem we have to shape the role and application more tightly: specify the overnight coverage need, keep the weekend terms highly visible, and make the assessment entirely revolve around the most predictive writing and handoff work.

strength: It gets the core story right from the data: we mainly lose to Semrush in agencies on reporting and PPC, while our biggest leak is our own Lite limits and plan friction.
mistake: It gives four moves instead of using the full room for five, and it ranks the AWT onboarding move above the Lite churn fix even though the Lite problem is the fastest money in the data.
to10: Put the Lite limit and pricing fix at #1, keep the focused agency reporting bet, and add one more tightly scoped move without losing the discipline of what not to build.

strength: It is clear, on-brand, and it explicitly says not to chase PPC parity while identifying agencies as the real competitive battleground.
mistake: It puts the reporting build ahead of the self-inflicted Lite churn problem, and Move 5 drifts into generic content advice instead of staying tightly on the owner’s asked-for Semrush response.
to10: Re-rank around the fastest, highest-confidence wins in our own data: Lite limits first, agency reporting second, AWT multi-site nurture third, then keep every move tied to a measurable Semrush or churn problem.

strength: It uses our actual data to drive the plan: retained users over installs, migration as the main launch risk, staged rollout, and early access for creators and extension authors.
mistake: It sends an early build to 300 power users on 16 November but then says the first move is Monday 16 November while the brief starts on Friday 13 November; more importantly, the 10% migration-ticket gate may be unrealistically strict and some projections are asserted a bit confidently.
to10: Tighten a few thresholds and assumptions, add explicit owners on every critical task, and make the creator/author outreach and support plan just slightly more concrete without adding complexity.

strength: It understands the core lesson that creators and extension authors are the best channels for users who stay, and it frames messages well for each audience.
mistake: It invents too much beyond the brief and asks for resources we do not have, especially 'engineers join support shifts' during freeze, a 1,000-beta-user requirement, and community Slack; it also makes weaker channel and rollout decisions than the data supports.
to10: Strip out assumptions that are not grounded in the brief, keep the plan sized to the actual team, make the rollout and launch timing simpler, and sharpen the launch-day assets to match our voice and principles more closely.

strength: It picks the right problem to solve, ties it to the churn data, and gives a concrete plan, test, math, risks, and customer message in our voice.
mistake: It dismisses yearly billing too quickly even though improving yearly uptake is one of the fastest near-term wins in our data, and a few revenue figures are a bit rough rather than tight.
to10: Tighten the math, include a simple honest yearly uptake change alongside the new plan or explain more clearly why not, and sharpen the downgrade/cannibalization assumptions with one cleaner sensitivity table.

strength: It also finds the right segment and gives a practical test with explicit go/stop rules and straightforward customer messaging.
mistake: The yearly price is wrong for our own pattern and some core revenue math is off, which makes me less confident in acting on the recommendation as written.
to10: Fix the pricing and revenue math, align the yearly discount with our existing structure, and make the cannibalization assumptions and month-6 impact fully traceable from our numbers.

strength: It reads the data the way I hoped: push hard into sleep, narrator clips, and evening posting, while staying inside team capacity and handling week 1 review constraints sensibly.
mistake: It includes a Wednesday 14:30 test that goes against the clear evening signal, and its weighted baseline/save-rate math is a bit too neat to fully trust without checking.
to10: Make week 1 and the recurring schedule even tighter around evening sleep content, keep the parent insight without giving up an off-peak slot, and tighten the KPI math.

strength: It strongly backs sleep and narrator clips and gives a usable structure with clear stop-doing recommendations.
mistake: It gets a key operating fact wrong by claiming sleep posts cannot run in week 1 and over-applies review to all sleep content, which distorts the plan and would make us miss easy wins.
to10: Handle review timing correctly, use week 1 for non-reviewed winding-down sleep content, clean up the factual slips, and then keep the strong sleep-first format mix.

strength: It is built around the two behaviors that matter most in our data—recurring tasks and a second device—and it uses the trigger limits correctly with sensible skips and branching.
mistake: It removes the Pro email entirely from onboarding and replaces it with a second recurring-task push, which is defensible but leaves revenue and upgrade timing less explored than it could.
to10: Keep this structure, but test whether email 5 should branch: recurring-task nudge for low-engagement users and a soft Pro email for users who already formed one or both key habits.

strength: It sounds like us, handles mobile vs web well, and the calm inactivity email is strong and on-brand.
mistake: It spends one of only five onboarding emails on a Pro pitch even though the strongest owner signal is to center the series on recurring tasks and second-device setup; that weakens the habit-building priority.
to10: Replace the Pro email with another habit-forming step tied to our proven retention behaviors, or make the fifth email branch so only highly engaged users get Pro while everyone else gets a second nudge toward recurring tasks or second-device use.

strength: It uses our data well: it spots that comparison pages drive trials, not blog traffic, and gives the team a concrete month-by-month plan plus a real first-week task list.
mistake: The priorities slip in places: a docs CTA projected at +25 trials is ranked below a cookie-banner rewrite projected at +3, and the high-intent cookie/cookieless pages are not both tackled immediately. It also has at least one risky factual claim about competitors' hosted/self-hosted options.
to10: Move the cookie-banner and cookieless analytics rewrites into week one or month one, fix the competitor fact issue, rank dev tasks by trial impact, and cut or justify the unproven new agency/import pages with search demand.

strength: It is tightly tied to trials, not traffic, with sensible math, conservative projections, ready-to-use titles, and clear day-60/day-90 rules the team can act on.
mistake: It is a little too hands-off with pages that already win, especially docs; I would still use high-ranking docs like WordPress to send more qualified visitors to trial. The cookie-banner rewrite could also come sooner.
to10: Add internal trial links from the strongest docs pages, bring the cookie-banner page into month one if capacity allows, and make the month-two comparison refresh list explicit so it cannot accidentally include pages we meant to leave alone.

strength: It picks the right segment, shows the seat math clearly, and builds the page around the recruiting buyer’s real pain: candidate scheduling back and forth plus fair interviewer load.
mistake: The sample-size and stop-rule detail is more than I need for the page brief, and the PTO/calendar wording needs a final product check before publishing.
to10: Tighten a few sections, keep every team CTA as “Book a demo,” and replace placeholder proof with real approved screenshots and customer proof.

strength: It is practical and well structured, with a strong test metric that avoids optimizing for low-quality signups.
mistake: It adds a few unsupported or risky claims, like three or four emails per interview, text reminders, and tool/video support, and it uses “Get started” in team sections where the brief says to use “Book a demo.”
to10: Remove unsupported claims, align all team CTAs to “Book a demo,” and move the page a little more tightly around round robin, routing, and security as the buying blockers.

strength: It spots the real story: database growth is mostly low-converting AI app-builder traffic, and that is driving the margin problem. The burn bridge and runway math are useful and clear.
mistake: The assumptions section reads like internal drafting notes, especially saying dates are proposals to confirm, so I would not send it exactly as written.
to10: Make it fully send-ready by removing internal caveats, tightening a few lines, and putting the Customer A loss even closer to the top alongside the margin miss.

strength: It is the most sendable investor email: the miss, margin drop, Customer A loss, and VP Sales ask are all visible early, and the asks are specific with dates and profiles.
mistake: It is a little less analytical on the margin issue than Output 1, and repeats 'we plan' where I would rather sound more decisive.
to10: Add the sharper AI-builder math from Output 1, including direct-created database growth and the margin-point impact, while keeping this structure and concise style.

strength: It follows the data tightly: Controllers/Heads of Finance at 50-300 person SaaS companies, timed to pricing-page changes, with no links and a clear expected reply-rate model.
mistake: It uses the 9-to-4-day proof in step 1 and repeats it often; I would rather keep step 1 more focused on the pricing-change pain and use proof later.
to10: Move the proof out of step 1, trim the repetition across steps, and make the Step 2 ask a little softer than a 20-minute walkthrough.

strength: It picks the right segment and trigger, explains the list rules clearly, and gives a practical reply-rate expectation without overclaiming.
mistake: The emails often have more than one ask and lean into SDR-style reply prompts like "reply yes" or "reply steps," which feels less like finance peer-to-peer copy.
to10: Reduce each email to one clean question, remove the extra content offers unless those assets are ready, and make the copy sound more like a Controller talking to another finance leader.

strength: It turns the data into the right hiring design: APAC/00:00-08:00 UTC coverage, weekend rotation stated plainly, writing as the main signal, and no resume/cover letter pile.
mistake: The application reply tests tone more than problem-solving because the candidate has no facts to work from, so it may not screen as strongly as it could before the longer exercise.
to10: Use a slightly more concrete customer scenario in the application, add an adjustment/accessibility note, and tighten a few lines so the post is completely publish-ready.

strength: The post is warm, direct, and very usable, and the scorecard clearly follows the data by giving written work almost all the weight.
mistake: The salary is not high enough in the post, and the application exercise gives away the diagnosis, which weakens the signal on finding the real problem.
to10: Move the $82,000 salary into the opening lines, remove the small tension between five-day weeks and summer four-day weeks, and make the application exercise test both writing and diagnosis without being tricky.

strength: It separates the real Semrush problem from our self-inflicted leaks, with good math and a focused agency-reporting response instead of a PPC parity chase.
mistake: The fifth move is weaker and more generic than the first four, and Lite limits could arguably be ranked first as the fastest money.
to10: Put the Lite limits fix first or make the ranking logic explicit, tighten the final content move into a sharper retention/acquisition play, and add a clearer dated framing for the survey and internal data.

strength: It is very clear, quantified, and turns the AWT multi-site segment into an immediately testable pipeline with controls and expected impact.
mistake: It ranks the agency client-reporting product last, even though that is the core place we lose to Semrush and the main strategic response the data points to.
to10: Re-rank by business impact rather than speed, put Lite limits and agency reporting at the top, tie the multi-site AWT nurture to the reporting product more directly, and keep enterprise as a secondary operational fix.

strength: It understands the two biggest launch risks: retained users come from creators/community, and the migration problem can swamp support if we do not gate it before launch.
mistake: The channel ranking is muddled: it says it ranks by users who stay, but puts extension authors ahead of X and Product Hunt below Hacker News despite the retained-user math.
to10: Fix the retained-user ranking, tighten the rollout/support plan so it fits the small team, and make the go/no-go criteria a little more practical while keeping the strong messaging drafts.

strength: It puts the right bets first: YouTube creators, extension authors, migration safety, staged rollout, support capacity, and clear no-go rules before the code freeze.
mistake: The migration gate is too soft at 95%; for our audience, losing hotkeys for even a small group is launch-blocking unless the issue is fixed, not just documented.
to10: Make migration carry-over a stricter gate, add a little more detail to the author/creator launch assets, and sharpen the launch email with named community credits once available.

strength: It targets the right problem: Essentials customers with 8+ channels, where churn and exit reasons clearly point to a flat agency-style plan with approvals.
mistake: It underplays yearly billing even though yearly uptake is low and churn is much lower; I would want that included as part of the first rollout, not pushed to a later test.
to10: Add a clear yearly-billing push in the recommendation, tighten the month-6 math, and make the test measure Team downgrade risk before a wider launch.

strength: It finds the main leak, gives one clear recommendation, includes the churn and downgrade math, and remembers to use yearly billing as part of the switch moment.
mistake: The revenue table is a little compressed and the base-case assumptions are doing a lot of work; I would want the math shown more plainly before sharing it with the board.
to10: Make the revenue bridge easier to audit, use revenue-per-invited-customer as the main test metric, and soften the Team downgrade exposure with a tighter eligibility rule or clearer guardrail.

strength: It reads like a usable plan for our actual constraints: sleep-heavy, narrator-led, mostly evening, within 6 posts a week and 4 edited clips, with strong week 1 drafts that avoid unnecessary review.
mistake: The review timing is a little conservative/confusing around approval on Monday 23 November versus going live Tuesday 24, which could affect the first post of week 2.
to10: Tighten the review calendar so week 2 is fully schedulable from Monday 23 November, and add a slightly more detailed week-by-week variation instead of one repeated weekly pattern.

strength: It correctly makes sleep and narrator clips the core of the plan and uses the install-per-post data well to justify the shift.
mistake: It wrongly assumes all sleep posts require clinical/legal review, which removes sleep from week 1 and delays the strongest content for no good reason.
to10: Use non-condition sleep/wind-down language in week 1, fix the review logic, keep the evening sleep posts live from the start, and soften a few captions so they feel more Headspace and less tactical.

strength: It builds the whole series around the two retention habits that matter most: recurring tasks and a second device, while using platform branching and the inactivity trigger well.
mistake: The routing rules assume some filtering and send suppression that should be confirmed in the email tool, and the second-device email could perhaps come earlier for users who have not made a recurring task.
to10: Tighten the exact send logic by user path, confirm each skip rule is supported, and make the day-7/day-14 success metric consistent with the first-week retention signal.

strength: It clearly reads the data, uses the supported triggers, branches by platform, and writes calm, usable copy with one main action per email.
mistake: It keeps a Pro email in onboarding, which pulls focus away from the two behaviors that drive retention and means many users may not actually receive a full 5-email onboarding series.
to10: Replace the Pro email with another habit-building email for users who still lack a recurring task or second device, and move Pro to a later engaged-user lifecycle campaign.

strength: It reads the data the right way and turns it into a capacity-fit plan: shift hard from blog content to comparison and cookie-free pages, with a concrete first week and realistic month-by-month schedule.
mistake: It leaves too much writer capacity in months 2 and 3 unspecified or lightly justified, and it underuses the chance to turn docs/internal linking into more trial capture from pages that already rank well.
to10: Tighten the forecast math page by page, fill all 12 content slots with clearer rationale, and add a sharper consolidation plan for decaying blog posts into the exact money pages.

strength: It gives a broader set of ideas, including migration and agency-focused pages that match real buyer objections, and it is easy to read.
mistake: It drifts away from the strongest evidence in the data by spending scarce capacity on net-new pages not supported by search demand, and some projections are overstated or too speculative for me to plan against confidently.
to10: Cut the lower-evidence pages, anchor every move to the query and conversion data we actually have, and bring the forecasts and monthly plan back inside a stricter trial-first prioritization.

strength: It picks the right segment with the right seat math and structures the page around the recruiting buyer's real pains in the right order, especially moving round robin, routing, and security up.
mistake: It overreaches a bit with claims like skipping anyone who is off and introduces a composite success metric that is smart but harder to operationalize than the owner asked for.
to10: Tighten any unverified product claims, simplify the deciding test metric to one cleaner recruiting-team conversion metric, and replace placeholders with real proof assets.

strength: It is very readable and disciplined, with strong owner-level judgment on what not to claim, good use of the data, and a sensible recruiting-specific page flow.
mistake: It says the homepage hero stays as it is when the brief asked for a homepage hero for this segment, and it includes a precise test sample size that does not look reliable enough to publish without validation.
to10: Make the recommendation fully answer the homepage-hero ask, remove or verify the traffic math for the test, and sharpen the proof around security near the main CTA.

strength: It reads like our brief: the bad news is up front, the three numbers come first, and it explains the AI app-builder growth as a margin problem instead of a vanity win.
