mistake: It adds a few conclusions that feel more analytical than investor-update simple, especially the margin math in point 1 and the assumptions block at the end, which make it a bit busier than needed.
to10: Tighten the wording slightly, remove the drafty assumptions section from the investor-facing email, and make one ask clearly the top priority with the VP Enterprise Sales role in New York.

strength: It is easy to read on a phone and does a good job stating the miss, the margin drop, Customer A, and the VP Sales hiring need in plain language.
mistake: The runway row in the table is wrong for September, which creates a trust problem in an investor update where the numbers have to be clean.
to10: Fix the runway error, tighten the asks so the VP Enterprise Sales intro is unmistakably the main one, and sharpen the causal link between AI-builder traffic, idle projects, and the gross margin drop.

strength: It aimed tightly at the right segment and moment, used the pilot numbers well, and turned them into a focused list strategy and sequence I could actually run.
mistake: It says no email carries a link, but step 2 asks for a 20-minute walkthrough rather than following the brief's likely preference for a softer low-friction ask; its projected meeting math is also a bit more speculative than necessary.
to10: Tighten the forecast to the proven pilot baseline, keep the CTA consistently low-friction across all steps, and remove any numbers that depend on assumptions beyond the data.

strength: It correctly chose Controllers/Heads of Finance after pricing-page changes and kept the copy plain, readable, and close to the requested voice.
mistake: Several emails break the 'one question and one ask' rule by using both a question and a separate reply instruction, and the projection that 1,900 loaded contacts would yield about 65 positive replies is not supported by the pilot math.
to10: Fix the CTA structure so each email has one clear ask, make the forecast fully consistent with the pilot rates, and sharpen the sequence so it feels more like a finance peer than a sales rep.

strength: It reads like us, uses the actual hiring data to drive the design, and directly fixes the three real problems: writing as the main signal, the overnight coverage gap, and the unclear weekend rotation.
mistake: It changes the role in the brief from recruitment marketing specialist to customer support specialist and adds some scheduling detail that may be more specific than we want to publish.
to10: Keep this structure and approach, but align the role title exactly to the brief and tighten any assumptions we would want to verify before publishing.

strength: It correctly spots the main signals in the data and turns them into a simpler application process with writing weighted highest.
mistake: It introduces extra video interviews, weakens the scorecard by making the application reply only part of a broad 'writing' bucket, and misses the stronger move of using a realistic application exercise tied to the specific typo-and-resend scenario.
to10: Make the application itself the core filter, use one realistic customer-reply task and a handoff task, keep interview weight low, and make the post even more candid about the exact hours and weekend rotation.

strength: It identifies the core truth in the data: we mainly lose to Semrush with agencies, while our biggest leak overall is our own Lite plan limits, and it turns that into a focused set of actions.
mistake: It underranks the agency reporting move behind enterprise and AWT onboarding, even though reporting is the clearest product gap tied to Semrush losses.
to10: Keep the same structure, but move the Lite fix and agency reporting to the top two slots, and tighten a couple of projections and labels so the hierarchy matches the business stakes even more clearly.

strength: It clearly explains where Semrush wins and explicitly says not to chase PPC parity, which is exactly the strategic discipline we need.
mistake: It puts the reporting build first and adds a content-marketing move that is weakly tied to the owner's ask, while the faster money from fixing Lite limits should be more prominent.
to10: Replace the content move with a tighter operational or pricing move, promote the Lite churn fix to the top, and make the impact math more conservative and directly tied to the supplied data.

strength: It uses our own data to set the plan: creators and extension authors first, migration as the main launch gate, and Product Hunt/HN delayed until after risk is lower.
mistake: It says channels are ranked by retention rate, but the brief asked to rank by what will bring users who stay; that should be ranked by retained users, where X is ahead of extension authors.
to10: Rank channels by retained users while still prioritizing creators and authors for efficiency, tighten the few threshold assumptions, and add explicit author credit in the email with real examples.

strength: It clearly sees that creators and extension authors are the best quality channels and keeps the messaging focused on carry-over, which is the real user fear.
mistake: It invents too much and asks for more than the team really has: 1,000 beta users, engineers joining support during freeze, Product Hunt on the next day, and several thresholds and operational details not grounded in the brief.
to10: Make the plan fit the actual team and dates, remove unsupported assumptions, fix the channel ranking logic, and turn the launch sequence into a tighter staged rollout with explicit go/no-go gates before freeze.

strength: It picks one clear move that matches the real leak in the data, shows usable revenue math, and respects our transparency and grandfathering commitments.
mistake: It dismisses yearly billing too quickly and has a few shaky numbers or assumptions around revenue estimates and feature details that would need checking before we publish.
to10: Tighten the math, explicitly add the low-risk yearly upsell as part of the same recommendation or rollout, and validate the plan design against likely Team cannibalization.

strength: It focuses on the right segment, names the main cannibalization risk clearly, and gives a practical test with go/stop thresholds.
mistake: The yearly price is inconsistent with our current pricing structure and the brief, and several numbers are off enough that I would not trust it without reworking the math.
to10: Use correct pricing math throughout, align the yearly price and promises with our model, and show a cleaner owner-level revenue case tied to the two-quarter window.

strength: It clearly sees the big opportunity: shift hard toward sleep, narrator clips, and evening posting, and it cuts low-value formats and themes.
mistake: It gets the review rule wrong by assuming all sleep posts need review and then says week 1 cannot run sleep, which is not what the brief says and leads to an overly restrictive week 1 plan.
to10: Keep the strong prioritization, but fix the review logic, make week 1 use non-review sleep/wind-down posts, and tighten the plan so channel mix and posting pattern feel more deliberate and immediately usable.

strength: It is easy to read, usable in structure, and the drafts sound warm and close to the brand voice.
mistake: It ignores the most important operating constraint and strategy signal: week 1 includes multiple sleep posts that would need review, and it keeps too much stress-at-work volume instead of pushing harder into sleep.
to10: Rebuild the schedule around the actual review timing, make narrator sleep clips the clear core of the plan, and cut stress-at-work further so the content mix follows the install data more decisively.

strength: It builds the whole series around the two behaviors most tied to retention, uses only triggers the tool actually supports, and cleanly branches by signup platform.
mistake: Email 5 repeats the recurring-task push instead of testing whether a later, segmented Pro message might be better for engaged users.
to10: Keep this structure, then tighten Email 5 by either segmenting it further or briefly justifying why a second recurring-task push beats a delayed Pro message for this onboarding window.

strength: The writing sounds on-brand and the platform-based second-device email is strong and useful.
mistake: It keeps a Pro email in the 5-email onboarding series and gives up the fifth slot that could have pushed one of the two retention-driving habits again.
to10: Replace the Pro email with another habit-building email tied to recurring tasks or second-device use, and make the success metrics center more clearly on both-habits adoption and day-30 retention.

strength: It follows the money: comparison pages and high-intent cookie queries get the writer slots, while general blog work is stopped.
mistake: The trial forecast is a little too confident, especially assuming a GA alternative page can reach Matomo-like CTR and that several developer tasks fit into one day.
to10: Make the first week include the cookie-banner rewrite/retitle alongside the GA comparison work, tighten the dev-day scope, and make forecasts more conservative with ranges.

strength: It is disciplined, realistic, and trial-focused, with clear first-week tasks, ready-to-use titles, and projections that do not overpromise.
mistake: It underuses the docs/internal-linking opportunity and says to leave some already-winning pages alone when a light factual refresh and links could protect and grow them.
to10: Add a stronger docs/internal-link plan, include the cookie-banner page earlier, and be clearer about which comparison pages get refreshed without contradicting the stop list.

strength: It picks the right segment, shows the seat math clearly, and builds the page around the real recruiting pain: ending email tennis with round robin and routing brought up early.
mistake: It uses some self-serve 'Get started' CTAs on a team recruiting page and includes a few claims/placeholders that need checking, like text reminders, PTO handling, integrations, and customer quotes.
to10: Use 'Book a demo' consistently for the team path, tighten any unsupported product claims, keep security proof closer to the first demo CTA, and replace all bracketed proof with real approved assets.

strength: It is very disciplined: the segment math is right, the page order matches the buyer journey, the claims are careful, and the voice feels practical and credible for recruiting teams.
mistake: The assumption that the homepage hero stays as it is is not ideal, because the brief asked for a hero version aimed at this segment and the current generic hero is part of the problem.
to10: Remove or revise the homepage assumption, add a little more concrete proof near the first CTA, and make the final page feel slightly more like finished marketing copy rather than an annotated wireframe.

strength: It leads with the three right numbers, puts the forecast miss, margin drop, Customer A, and VP Sales problem where investors will see them, and gives specific dated asks.
mistake: The Customer A response is a little light; asking for a review is useful, but I would want a clearer owner and retention/learning plan.
to10: It is already very close; the only improvement would be adding a concrete owner and date for the Customer A post-mortem, plus a measured expected savings range from the 48-hour pause once modeled.

strength: It does the best job explaining the AI-builder problem, including direct-created database growth and the margin impact of the extra compute cost.
mistake: It is less send-ready: it says the New York base and dates need confirmation, and it promises reporting the real saving in November even though the engineering change may not give a full-month read by then.
to10: Remove the draft caveats, move the full metric table closer to the top or make the first screen tighter, and change the compute-saving language to report after the first full month post-ship.

strength: It reads the pilot correctly: Controllers/Heads of Finance at 50-300 person SaaS companies, timed to pricing-page changes, with no links in step 1 and a grounded reply-rate forecast.
mistake: The copy leans a little too much on reply-keyword asks like “reply yes” and “reply steps,” which feels more like a sales sequence than a finance peer-to-peer note.
to10: Tighten the CTAs so each email has one natural finance-person ask, move the proof out of step 1 or make it less prominent, and avoid depending on a one-page summary/three-step asset that was not provided.

strength: The email copy sounds the most like a finance person writing to another finance person: specific, plain, and tied to pricing changes, rev rec, close, audit timing and engineering ownership.
mistake: The reply-rate forecast is a little optimistic with the 7%-10% range and the 1.25x assumption; I would rather anchor closer to 6.8%-7.9% until tested.
to10: Make the forecast more conservative, add slightly clearer one-ask CTAs in steps 1 and 4, and keep the meeting ask in step 2 a touch softer.

strength: It understands the core of the hire: cover the 00:00 to 08:00 UTC gap, lead with writing, remove experience requirements, state the weekend rotation plainly, and put the salary right up front in a calm 37signals voice.
mistake: The application reply tests tone more than problem-solving because the applicant has no facts to work with; I’d rather give them a small real clue so we can see whether they fix the actual issue.
to10: Use a slightly more realistic application exercise with enough information to solve the customer’s problem, and tighten the hiring steps so the first written sample and later exercise map exactly to the scorecard.

strength: The scorecard and application exercise are very strong: the Priya example tests clear writing and actual problem-solving, and the weights reflect the data instead of old hiring habits.
mistake: The job post does not put the salary in the first screen, and a few bits feel more like an HR template than us, especially the time-zone table and the scam warning line.
to10: Move pay and terms near the top, warm up the voice, trim the process language, and make the post feel less procedural while keeping the excellent application exercise and scorecard.

strength: It finds the real pattern in the data: Semrush is mainly an agency/reporting/PPC problem, while our bigger leak is Lite limits and pricing friction. The per-1,000 and churn math is useful and owner-ready.
mistake: The ranking is more 'quickest money per effort' than 'impact,' so the agency reporting bet ends up fourth even though it is the main competitive issue against Semrush.
to10: Move Lite limits to the top or make the ranking logic explicit, and put the agency Monday report higher as the main competitive response. Tie the AWT multi-site nurture directly to that report.

strength: It gives the competitive answer cleanly: we lose agencies on reporting and PPC, should not chase PPC parity, and should fix Lite limits plus multi-site AWT onboarding. The ranked moves have owners, first steps, and metrics.
mistake: The fifth move, content built on link data, is weaker and more generic than the other four, with less direct connection to the Semrush problem.
to10: Replace or sharpen the content move with a more measurable retention/acquisition action, and make the Lite-limit fix feel as urgent as the agency reporting build.

strength: It understands the real launch risk: don't break hotkeys, prove migration before launch, prepare support, and put creators/authors ahead of broad-reach channels.
mistake: The channel ranking table is not actually ranked by retained users: X and Product Hunt kept more users than extension authors in the raw numbers, even though authors deserve more strategic attention because of retention quality and upside.
to10: Fix the channel ranking and rationale, make the support plan more realistic than borrowing engineers during freeze, and tighten the go/no-go gates into a smaller, owner-ready checklist.

strength: It makes the right strategic call: creators, authors, staged rollout, migration before code freeze, and Product Hunt/Hacker News as secondary reach instead of the centerpiece.
mistake: It says the channel table is ranked by users who stay, but actually ranks by retention rate; the absolute retained-user math needs to be named more carefully.
to10: Clarify absolute retained users versus retention rate, make the 95% migration gate stricter for any lost hotkeys/settings, and specify exactly when the full existing-user email goes to each rollout wave.

strength: It picks the right problem and one clear fix: Essentials customers with 8+ channels are churning because per-channel pricing stops feeling fair, and a flat Agency plan directly answers that.
mistake: It underplays yearly billing and does not measure Team cannibalization until after launch, even though both are important to the two-quarter revenue goal.
to10: Add a simple, honest yearly-billing prompt as part of the launch, and include Team 8+ customers in the test so we know the downgrade risk before putting Agency on the public pricing page.

strength: It sees both big levers: fixing the 8+ Essentials churn problem and using yearly billing more honestly at the moment customers switch.
mistake: The revenue math is less trustworthy than it needs to be, especially the month-6 impact, and the 2-user Agency plan may invite more Team downgrades than necessary.
to10: Tighten the revenue model so every number ties out, make the Team cannibalization guard stronger, and simplify the customer wording so it feels more like our plain pricing voice.

strength: It follows the strongest business signals: much more sleep content, narrator audio as the core format, evening posting, and a clear stop list for quote cards, app news, focus/productivity and morning posts.
mistake: It over-applies review to all sleep content, so week 1 becomes all kindness and misses the chance to post non-condition wind-down content right away. It also gets the earliest review timing a bit too conservative.
to10: Use week 1 for sleep/wind-down posts that avoid naming conditions, keep narrator clips central, and tighten the review plan so only posts that mention conditions go through clinical/legal review.

strength: The drafts feel warm, simple and on-brand, and it uses customer language well, especially the email replay, pickup and day-three drop-off moments.
mistake: The plan does not push sleep hard enough given the install data, keeps a weekly stress-at-work slot, and has a review/calendar conflict around week 2 Monday if those posts need approval.
to10: Shift more of the mix from stress/kindness into sleep narrator clips, give a clearer 4-week calendar with specific post angles, and make the review timing airtight.

strength: It builds the whole series around the two actions that matter most for retention: recurring tasks and a second device, while keeping the voice calm and practical.
mistake: A few trigger rules need tightening, especially the second-device email timing and the fact that some users may not receive five emails if they already complete the key actions.
to10: Make the branching and suppression logic fully implementation-ready, and add exact measurement windows for each goal action without mixing day 7 and day 14 comparisons.

strength: It clearly understands the retention signals and writes simple, on-brand emails around repeats, second device use, and a gentle inactivity nudge.
mistake: It keeps a Pro email in the onboarding series, even though the data says the early upgrade email performs poorly and causes unsubscribes; that space should stay focused on habit formation.
to10: Replace the Pro email with another habit-building email, tighten the goal measurement, and avoid introducing paid-feature education before users have fully built trust in the list.

strength: Ranks by trials with a clean ceiling table, names the cookie-banner post as Maya's own question, and gives a real Monday-to-Friday writer list.
mistake: The cookie-banner rewrite is valued at the blog rate (+3 trials) instead of being scored on its intent to hand off to /privacy-focused-web-analytics, which undersells the strongest Maya-surface play; also ranks /vs-google-analytics first when the cookie pages better match her phrase.
to10: Reorder so the two cookie pages come before the GA comparison, value the banner post by assisted trials to the cookie-free page, and add one line on which old blog posts get merged or redirected first.

strength: Says what to stop, leaves /vs-matomo and the WordPress doc alone, gives ready-to-use titles and meta in our voice, and adds day-60/day-90 decision rules so the plan survives without me.
mistake: Slightly conservative on the GA comparison (+19 to +46 vs the +100 ceiling) and buries the cookie-banner post in Month 2, so Maya's fastest win lands a month late.

strength: Segment math is explicit and correct (about 1,540 of 2,717 paid seats), and the page reorders sections around what paying recruiting accounts actually use: round robin, routing, security up from the footer, and a 4-field demo form.
mistake: Hero A buries Priya's own words ("email tennis") in section 2 while the headline uses the tamer "back and forth"; the test also spends a lot of text on a sample-size calculation that risks looking over-engineered for a copy brief.
to10: Put "email tennis" in the hero itself, tighten the test section to one sentence on the deciding metric, and mark every proof point clearly as an example so nothing reads as a real customer claim.

strength: Hero leads with "No email tennis" in Priya's exact words, and the page keeps the voice tight and human; the bracket convention for unverified facts is a mature way to ship without inventing proof.
mistake: Mixes "Get started" (self-serve) and "Book a demo" buttons across almost every section with no logic, adds a separate open-source section and a problem section that pad length, and the bracket placeholders mean it is not publishable as it stands.
to10: Pick one CTA per stage (demo for the recruiting page, self-serve only in the tail), fold open source into security as supporting proof, drop the redundant problem section into the hero, and resolve placeholders so it can ship.

strength: Honest, specific, and structured like a builder's update: three numbers, bad news up front, burn explained, and concrete asks with dates and profiles.
mistake: The cost math in 'What went wrong' is confusing and slightly speculative ('On about $10.4M of monthly revenue, that extra $0.9M is roughly 9 points of margin, more than the 7-point drop'), and the closing assumptions about meeting dates need to be resolved before sending.
to10: Tighten the cost explanation to say plainly what the $0.9M free-tier compute did to gross margin and what the 48-hour pause is expected to recover, and resolve the internal assumptions (New York base, ask dates) so no caveats are needed.

strength: Very clean structure: headline numbers, bad news, a forwardable ask at the top, and a table with runway change; it reads like a candid, specific investor update from a builder.
mistake: It introduces a 'runway at that month's burn' row comparing September and October (52 months to 33 months) that wasn't asked for and could confuse readers; also the forwardable line for ask 1 feels a bit like a pitch.
to10: Drop the extra runway comparison row or explain it, and keep the asks even sharper without the forwardable snippet, so the whole email feels less like marketing.

strength: Nails the segment, the pricing-change trigger and the no-link rule, and every email reads like a finance peer writing to another finance peer.
mistake: Step 1 still contains a soft second element (the 9-to-4 proof plus the 'reply yes' ask) that pushes it toward two asks and slightly over the 120-word discipline; also the subject options are lowercase and a touch casual for a controller.
to10: Tighten step 1 to one question and one ask under 120 words with a cleaner subject line, and put the 9-to-4 proof cleanly in step 2 only.

strength: Sharpest structure and the honest 7-10% range with a worked projection table, plus a clean stop-on-reply and gating rule.
mistake: The 8% point estimate and 25% uplift are an invented multiplier not supported by the pilot, and it risks over-promising; step 1 also names Chargebee and stacks proof, question and context, edging past the 'one ask' feel and grade-8 plainness.
to10: Anchor the expectation at 6.8-7.9% without the 1.25x uplift, and make step 1 leaner and link-free with no product name until step 2.

strength: Reads exactly like us: $82,000 in the first line, the weak hours owned plainly, the weekend rotation stated with its reason, and a warm welcome to teachers and hotel people without a whiff of HR template.
mistake: The 'why this job?' 100-word prompt edges toward a cover letter in disguise and isn't tied to any signal in our data; the post itself is tightly on-brand but the scorecard leans a bit on a second exercise the post only vaguely describes.
to10: Drop or replace the 'why this job' question with something scored, and add the scorecard weights' checks against the data sentence so a reviewer can see why each number exists.

strength: The hours-by-city table, the Priya application prompt with a real typo to catch, and the 03:00 UTC shortlist exercise are genuinely sharp — the prompts do real work and show what good looks like.
mistake: Voice drifts toward HR-process polish in places ('Need an adjustment, like more time? We will never ask you for money', the numbered hiring funnel with dates) and 85% weighting is stated as a rule before the weights add up to the table, which reads slightly like a template.
to10: Tighten the voice to sound like a person in the post (trim the procedural lines), and make the weighting math and 'pass or fail' clear in one place rather than scattered.

strength: Correctly frames the Lite usage-limit leak as the biggest self-inflicted loss and puts the multi-site Webmaster Tools fix first with a clean holdout design and named owning teams.
mistake: Places the agency client-report bet last largely on build-time logic, which slightly buries the one product gap that matters most long-term, and it drops the brief's exact 'no more than five' to four with a couple of loose presentational choices.
to10: Keep the four sharp moves but reframe move four's priority honestly (impact-plus-timing, not just 'takes longest'), and tighten the projected-lift assumptions so every number carries a date-stamped source or is clearly flagged as a planning guess.

strength: Crisp short-answer framing, a clean per-100-trials math walkthrough, and the Lite cliff and multi-site AWT wins all present with owners and first steps.
mistake: Ranks the agency client report first and the cheaper, faster Lite fix second, which inverts the brief's own 'fastest money' logic, and the invented 'November 2026' datestamp sits oddly against test data with no such date.
to10: Reorder so the Lite usage-limit fix runs first as the cheapest win, fix or remove the fabricated 'data as of' datestamp, and trim move five (content studies) since it is the one move with the weakest number behind it and drifts toward generic advice.

strength: It does the hard thinking the data demands: ranks channels by retained users with the math, treats the 58% migration problem as the central risk, waves the rollout with a stop rule, and gates launch on carry-over tests before the code freeze.
mistake: Voice slips in a couple of places: 'Bad news to fix first' reads slightly off-brand, and the X post is thinner than the email; the launch-day post could carry a bit more of the craft and community warmth the email shows.
to10: Tighten voice consistency across the X post and plan copy, add a named community-credit moment on launch day (an author roll call), and put the X post's 'press ⌥ Space and watch' next to an explicit 'will my hotkeys work' line in the first post rather than only in the email.

strength: Voice and craft are excellent: the email and the five-part X thread sound like Raycast, credit authors by name, show the shortcut, and directly answer the 'will my setup move' fear; the multi-post X structure with recordings matches the 'show it moving' principle.
mistake: It spreads launch across too many days and channels and asks for more simultaneous work than a small team can do: Show HN and full email and creators and authors all at 16:00 on 8 Dec, Product Hunt on 9 Dec, four-plus X posts, plus a 1,000-person beta, daily engineering support shifts, and a claims list — it's ambitious for one launch manager, one designer, one editor and 3 support staff, and some gates (1,000 beta users, zero losses) are stricter than the team can realistically prove by 4 Dec.
to10: Cut scope to what the team can actually run: fewer dated commitments, a simpler staged-rollout gate, a realistic beta size, and consolidate the launch-day surface so the small team can execute it flawlessly.

strength: The customer message is pure Buffer: honest, plain, shows the customer's own bill next to the new price and explicitly says 'Happy on Essentials? Stay.' It reads like us.
mistake: Quotes the churn bleed slightly low ($23,900) versus the owner's own $24,700; small but it's a number the owner checks, and the 1-user Agency limit may frustrate the very freelancers it targets.
to10: Exact bleed math, a 2-user allowance consistent with freelancers' needs, and a cleaner two-quarter net figure with the yearly-upside path quantified.

strength: Nails the owner's priorities: identifies the 8+ Essentials leak, quantifies churn-driven value, guards Team cannibalization with a break-even ('loses money if more than 1 in 3 Team 8+ move down'), and includes a downside case.
mistake: The yearly price is internally inconsistent: $66/mo billed yearly is a big discount vs. $79, but the switch math uses $76.53 blended—an owner reading closely will stumble on which number is real, and the email shows '$66 a month' next to '$79' without explaining the trade-off.
to10: Reconcile the yearly price and blended math, tighten the tables so the month-6 gain is obvious, and polish the customer voice to match Buffer's grade-7 clarity.

strength: It gets the data story right and builds a practical, warm plan around it: sleep at night, narrator clips, a week 1 that needs no review, and drafts that sound like us.
mistake: It under-uses the parent audience after week 1 (only one parent-focused post a week), and it calls the Wednesday 14:30 pickup slot a test without explaining how it will be evaluated against the evening baseline.
to10: Give the parent audience more than one post, and use the review timing more aggressively by submitting all sleep posts on 16 November and planning week 2 sleep posts from 24 November, not just week 1.

strength: It is clear about the review constraint and correctly identifies that sleep posts need review, so it front-loads kindness in week 1 and submits sleep posts early.
mistake: It plans no sleep posts until 24 November, which wastes the first week for the highest-install theme, and it leans too heavily on kindness in week 1, which is weaker than sleep and less aligned with the young professional's nighttime pain point.
to10: Fill week 1 with sleep-adjacent posts that avoid named conditions (e.g., winding down, switching off) and submit them for review on 16 November, so sleep content can start from 24 November, while still keeping a parent post and a kindness post for range.

strength: Calm, on-brand voice throughout, with each email carrying one tip, one button, real-screen screenshot notes and quoted typed examples; goals and measures are stated per email and the drop list is quantified.
mistake: Email 5 (Pro) is gated only on having a habit and still pitches an upgrade inside onboarding, and the day-3 second-device email doesn't build on whether the recurring-task habit is already in place; the series is also slightly less precise about triggering email 2/3 off events rather than fixed days.
to10: Tighten the trigger logic (skip/swap on each habit event, not just one), state the platform split percentages explicitly, and either move Pro fully out of onboarding or justify its day-14 gated placement with a target.

strength: Most rigorous trigger design: event-triggered emails with skip rules, an at-a-glance goals/measures table, a day-10 fallback for users who never made a recurring task, and explicit platform percentages (59%/41%).
mistake: Voice slips slightly from the brief (subject 'Type it once. Todoist repeats it.' and 'Three tasks you'll never retype' lean clever/promotional, and email 4's copy is thinner), and email 5 repeats the recurring-task ask already covered by email 2, so the range of habits is narrower.
to10: Warm the subject lines and email 4 body back to the calm brand voice, and diversify the fifth email (e.g. a second-device or Today-view habit) so the series isn't two pushes at the same behavior.

strength: It ranks by trials per 1,000 clicks using my own numbers, shows the arithmetic, and is honest that the 44,000-impression cookie post is a clicks win not a trials win. Ready-to-use titles and metas plus a day-by-day week 1 mean the writer starts Monday without me.
mistake: Sequencing: week 1 and the top of the ranking go to the hardest page (/vs-google-analytics) while the two cheap cookie-intent wins wait until week 4 and month 2, so there is no fast result to show. It also spends 5 of 12 writer slots on alt-page refreshes with no trial forecast, and claims move 5 adds the most clicks when move 1's top end (+1,450) beats it (+1,230).
to10: A month-by-month trial forecast with the lag spelled out, the cookie-banner rewrite and cookies-page retitle inside week 1, a forecast attached to the 7 alt-page refreshes, and month 3's two TBD slots named rather than left to day-60 rules.

strength: More different ideas than the other plan, and two good ones: a trial prompt on the docs template (24,600 clicks at 4.8 per 1,000) and a page for Maya's real blocker, moving off GA4 without losing history. The opening trials-per-1,000 table is the clearest read of my data of the two.
mistake: The ranking contradicts its own numbers: rank 5 (+25 trials) sits below rank 3 (+20) and rank 4 (+3). It also sells a 175-trials-a-month ceiling built on a 9% CTR borrowed from "matomo vs plausible" and applied to "google analytics alternative" at top 3, which I don't believe, and it hands the redirect audit to a "strategist" I don't employ.
to10: Rank strictly by the trials column, give ranges and timing instead of one ceiling, use a defensible CTR for the head term, drop the phantom strategist, measure trials by landing page monthly as asked rather than every Friday, and give week 1 the same day-by-day "done when" rigour the other plan has.

strength: Picks recruiting with the seat math, then builds the page around Priya's email-tennis pain, round robin and routing proof, and moves security up without hype.
mistake: Security sits one section too far from the demo, and the A/B sample-size math borrows the page's 3.1% signup baseline for a demo-request metric.
to10: Put security proof immediately beside the demo form, add real recruiting customer proof and screenshots, and tie the A/B test math to the demo-request baseline.

strength: Same sharp recruiting seat math, a strong 'No email tennis' hero, and a thoughtful qualified-team-start metric.
mistake: Gives open source its own full section despite 7% survey weight, and mixes 'Get started' CTAs into a team page that should drive demos.
to10: Cut the open-source section to supporting proof, use 'Book a demo' consistently, remove unsupported no-show/SMS claims, and keep routing and security close to the demo form.

strength: It is a working system, not a document: a publishable post with the hard parts first, the UTC window translated into readers' own clocks, a real Priya ticket with a findable cause, a 03:00 UTC second-round exercise, two call questions, anchored 1/3/5 rows, blind read with calibration, and the weekend rotation repeated at offer. I could hand this to three reviewers on Monday.
mistake: Buries the $82,000 in "Pay and terms" below the hard parts, when the whole point was to publish the salary in the first screen, and adds a line ("We will never ask you for money") that sounds like a gig-scam notice, not us.
to10: Lead with the salary and the hours in the first three lines, cut that odd money line, and add an explicit hiring threshold (e.g. 4.0 overall with no row under 3) so reviewers stop arguing about the edge cases.

strength: The opening line does the job — "$82,000 a year, the same wherever you live" — and the reviewer-time arithmetic is the sharpest thinking in either answer: 160 hours is 4.6 minutes an application, 2 minutes a reply is 70 hours, about 23 each, plus 7 for second reads. That is the number I would actually take to the team.
mistake: The scorecard grades a "longer written exercise" it never writes, gives no call questions, and asks every applicant for a 100-word "why this job" that nothing scores — so the hiring team still has homework before it can run, and we add reading time for no signal.
to10: Write the second-round exercise itself (a real overnight ticket plus the handoff note), add the two call questions and a calibration set, and either drop the "why this job" question or give it a scored row — then it runs as-is.

strength: It answers the brief the way an operator wants it: a glance table with goal and measure per email, skip rules, real trigger logic off the recurring-task event, subject lines with character counts, and a drop table that puts a number on every cut.
mistake: It deletes the Pro email outright and spends the fifth slot re-pitching recurring tasks, so the series has no path to paid conversion and the last email repeats email 2.
to10: Keep a calm Pro email at day 14 for users who already made a recurring task or added a second device (replace the duplicate recurring nudge), and fix the one loose target: both habits is 8% by day 7, so measure it at day 7, not day 14.

strength: Commercially the smarter shape: it keeps a gentle Pro email but moves it to day 14 for engaged users only, and the five emails cover more distinct ground (empty the head, repeats, second device, calm restart, Pro) with simpler sequencing.
mistake: Loose production detail — no subject-line length checks, and 'sign in with this email' is the kind of small inaccuracy that ships; the second-device email also sits on a fixed day 3 rather than using the recurring-task trigger to time it.
to10: Add per-email skip rules and a at-a-glance table with goal and measure, verify subject lengths and fix the sign-in wording, and trigger the second-device email off the recurring-task event so the sequence builds habit on habit.

strength: A genuinely usable plan: the Week 1 day-by-day writer brief, the 'stop' list, and a ranked table with trial math tied to my own conversion rates.
mistake: The cookie-banner rewrite is ranked 4th but gets a whole writer slot in Month 1 while the position-11.4 cookies page waits until Month 2; also the 'trial prompt on docs pages' figure (about +25 trials) is hand-waved and the +100 trials from top-3 on /vs-google-analytics assumes a CTR jump I haven't proven.
to10: Put the two high-impression, near-page-one pages (cookie banner post and cookies page) earlier and paired so the blog post feeds the product page within the same month, and tighten the ceilings so the forecast shows a low/high band instead of a single confident number.

strength: Reads like it came from someone who actually looked at my numbers: the blog-only decline framing, trials-per-1,000 comparison, ready-to-use titles and metas, 'leave the winners alone' rule, and day-60/day-90 decision rules.
mistake: The month-by-month writer allocation is a bit vague later ('2 pages set by the day-60 rules'), and the +19 to +46 projection on /vs-google-analytics is still a wide guess; one or two of the range estimates feel padded.
to10: Lock all 12 pages by name across the three months (no 'to be decided at day 60'), give the docs trial-prompt idea the developer slot it deserves given the WordPress doc's 21% CTR, and keep the titles/metas but add the trial forecast per month in the plan table too.

strength: Picks recruiting with the seat math in two lines, uses Priya's phrase, and puts security up with the demo button. Every section has its proof named.
mistake: The A/B variants are two sides of the same idea (pain vs feature) rather than pain vs outcome, and the reminder section claims nothing beyond the data but still reads a little thin.
to10: A second hero that tests a genuinely different promise (e.g. outcome: 'fill your interview slots without chasing anyone') and one named, permissioned customer quote in the round robin section instead of a placeholder.

strength: Nine sections with richer visuals, text/SMS reminders, reschedule-from-link, and a careful 'fill or cut' approach to facts it doesn't have.
mistake: Too many CTAs alternate between 'Get started' and 'Book a demo' on a page aimed at teams, and a standalone open source section leads a recruiter away from the pain. Metrics are muddier (qualified team starts) than a clean demo-request rate.
to10: Cut open source to a proof line, make every button 'Book a demo', trim to the owner's seven sections, and land on one clean deciding metric with a stop rule.

strength: Leads with the three numbers including the missed forecast and margin drop, puts Customer A up front, and explains the burn split and runway range cleanly. The self-hosting-leavers ask is a genuinely sharp investor ask.
mistake: The 'about 9 points of margin' math is a loose back-of-envelope tied to a $10.4M monthly revenue assumption; it invites a CFO to poke at it. Also slightly over 700 words with the assumptions block.
to10: Tighten to under 700 words, replace the 9-point margin estimate with the plain $0.9M compute figure, and make the Customer-A-learning ask name a person/team and date.

strength: Very readable; correct runway figures; forwardable blurb in ask 1 is a nice practical touch, and the 33 vs 37 month runway contrast is clear.
mistake: The runway table row comparing 52 vs 33 months is apples-to-oranges and confusing; also leads 'the bad news' with margin rather than Customer A and the missed forecast, burying the forecast miss in the top block only.
to10: Fix the runway comparison row, put the forecast miss and Customer A ahead of the margin story, and add the burn-split table so the $5.5M underlying number is visible.

strength: Locks onto the winning segment and trigger with the pilot numbers exposed, and projects an honest, defensible reply range instead of a wish.
mistake: Voice slips in step 2 and 3 (long explanatory lines that don't sound like a finance peer), and the 10% ceiling math is a bit generous given the two factors were never tested together.
to10: Tighten step 2 and 3 to one question and one ask in a finance person's cadence, and replace the 'x1.25' assumption with a clearly stated single base case plus a simple test plan.

strength: Voice is the best match to the brief and the 4,100-excluded / capacity math shows real operational thinking for the list.
mistake: Breaks the one-ask rule repeatedly (reply 'yes', reply 'steps', then 'now' or 'later', plus calendar-link-style CTAs) and miscounts by excluding pilot contacts as if they were in the new 6,000 list; the 9-day/4-day proof in step 4 is vague ('the close I shared is the reason I wrote').
to10: Enforce one question and one ask per email with no reply-keyword mechanics, fix the list arithmetic so exclusions match the actual 6,000 contacts, and ground the expected reply rate in a single stated base rate with an explicit test plan.

strength: Every element ties directly to our data and brand: the writing exercise replaces the cover letter, the scorecard weights writing 50% and drops culture fit, the post states the weekend rotation and the Asia-Pacific hours plainly, and the application plan cuts reviewer hours from 160 to 70.
mistake: The assumption about reviewer time (2 minutes per reply) could have been stated more prominently as an owner input, but it's minor.
to10: Nothing significant—maybe a slightly warmer opening line in the post to match our voice even more closely.

strength: The detailed time zone table and the concrete shortlist exercise scenario are excellent, practical touches that make the hiring process very clear.
mistake: The scorecard weights written work at 85%, which is higher than the correlation suggests and might over-index on writing at the expense of problem-solving; also, the assumption about reviewer time is buried in the projection.
to10: Rebalance the scorecard weights to give more room to problem-solving (from 30% to 35%) and reduce written work to 80%, and state the reviewer time assumption up front.

strength: Builds the whole argument from our own numbers: the per-1,000 trial table that shows agencies are 60% of Semrush losses, the Lite churn made explicit as 70% of monthly churn, and each move with an owning team, a first step this month, a success metric and one named assumed input. The blunt voice ('Our biggest customer leak is not Semrush. It is our own Lite plan') is exactly ours.
mistake: Its headline 'First move this month' is the Webmaster Tools onboarding track, while its own ranking puts the Lite top-up faster money; and ranking the agency reporting build last undercuts the 'where we lose is agencies' answer. The two rankings contradict each other.
to10: Make one ranking do the work: lead with the Lite usage-limit fix as fastest money, then the agency reporting bet as the strategic response to the only real Semrush loss, and keep the WMT nurture tied to it. Cut a couple of the percentage-point hedge chains so the numbers read faster.

strength: Reads cleanly and puts the agency reporting move first, which matches the data pattern; the Lite analysis ('only 37% of a Lite group is still with us after 12 months', the limit causing about a third of all monthly churn) is sharp, and the 'what we should not do' section is honest and fair to Semrush.
mistake: Move 5, 'teach with our link data', is generic content advice with a weak success metric (in-house share of trials) and no clear number behind it, exactly the kind of filler the brief said would annoy the owner. It also states 'Data as of November 2026', a date I never gave.
to10: Drop move 5 and replace it with something funded by the numbers, such as a dedicated agency trial tied to the multi-site Webmaster Tools group. Tighten move 1's first step so it has one owner and one measurable first-week action, and don't invent a data date I didn't supply.

strength: Does exactly what I asked: ranked channels by retained users with the math, made migration a hard gate before the 1 December freeze, and answered 'will my hotkeys still work' in both the X post and the email.
mistake: The five-post X thread violates my own brand principle of one keyboard shortcut per message and buries the single strongest fact; also the retention math is right but they didn't project the upside of giving all 9 creators and 1,500 authors early access, so the plan sells the biggest lever short.
to10: One tight launch post (not five), the YouTube upside projected like Output 2 does, and the no-go rule spelled out as clearly as 'if 1, 2 or 3 fails, existing users don't ship'.

strength: Owner-grade judgment throughout: re-ranks by retention, puts Product Hunt/Hacker News on a separate day with the numbers to justify it, projects the creator upside (~6,800 retained users), stages the rollout with a clear no-go rule, and writes copy I'd actually send.
mistake: Leaves the 1,500 authors' and 300 power users' early-access asks slightly under-specified (a share-kit date slips to 30 Nov but no share-kit contents), and 'watch' in the X post is a touch cute versus 'show it moving' — minor.
to10: Name one keyboard shortcut and one measured speed claim with the Mac in the launch post only after 27 Nov, and add a one-line share-kit contents list so authors know exactly what to post on day one.

strength: Picks one plan, targets the 8+ churn leak, shows the downside case and the 1-in-3 Team downgrade break-even, and the customer email is genuinely in our voice with the 'here's exactly what you'd pay' line.
mistake: Some numbers drift from my data (8+ Essentials at $249k vs my ~$257k; it folds the yearly discount into an average price per channel without showing the work), and it skips the yearly-by-default push as a lever even though it flags the 0.9% vs 4.0% churn on yearly payers.
to10: Tie the revenue math explicitly to my figures, show churn-reduction value month by month inside the two-quarter window, and make the cheap yearly-default test a named second action rather than a footnote.

strength: Owner-grade structure: bad news first, named assumptions, a 1,000-customer cohort table with three churn scenarios, the Team-downgrade ratio math, a clear go/stop rule and an invite email that reads like us with the exact-price line and the 'inviting in two groups' honesty.
mistake: The yearly payback argument ('pays back only around month 11') is a bit hand-wavy and contradicts its own note that yearly payers churn at 0.9%; the $23,900 lost-revenue figure is slightly off my ~$24,700, and the 1-user limit makes it less attractive to the freelancers it targets.
to10: Fix the yearly math to show the real payback (holding a yearly payer vs monthly), state the flat price more generously to freelancers (2 users), and reconcile the lost-revenue figure to my table.

strength: Gets all three data signals right and turns them into a clean 6-post week: sleep-led mix, narrator clips 4 a week, evening times, and a week 1 that needs no review while weeks 2-4 go in on 16 November.
mistake: Drafts are mostly sleep and kindness; no draft for the Friday stress-at-work carousel that stays in the plan, so that slot is a plan line only. Also the 14:30 parent slot jars slightly against the evening finding.
to10: Add the seventh draft for the Friday stress carousel (or swap it for a parent evening idea), and show the success measure per theme versus the exact baseline save rate so the bar is provable.

strength: Sharp reading of the numbers (installs per post, format gaps, stop list) and a fuller calendar with weekly angles, plus honest assumptions and a per-week install projection.
mistake: Treats every sleep post as needing review, so week 1 is all kindness and the first sleep post is 24 November; that throws away a week of our best theme and leaves only 15 sleep posts. The review rule only bites when a post names a condition.

strength: Centers the whole series on the two habits (recurring task + second device, 67% retention) with platform branching and trigger-based skips, and a clean drop table with numbers.
mistake: Email 5 sends a second 'recurring task' ask to people who already did email 2 — redundant, and it largely repeats email 2's tip instead of opening a new behavior.
to10: Replace email 5 with a genuinely new step (e.g., a gentle 'share your list' or 'plan your week' habit) rather than a repeat, and add one line on subject-line character counts being checked.

strength: Strong voice and genuine range — guilt-free check-in, platform-split device email, and a Pro email gated to engaged users only, with a holdout and unsubscribe guardrail.
mistake: Keeps a Pro upsell in a series meant to build two habits; the email is fine but spends a scarce onboarding slot on revenue instead of the retention behaviors the data says matter.
to10: Swap the Pro slot for a habit-building fifth email (or drop it), and make the trigger logic explicit about ordering when multiple triggers fire.

strength: A specific, capacity-aware plan with extra useful moves: docs trial prompt, GA4 migration page, and agency page, plus a real week-one writer list.
mistake: Its 'ranked by trials' table puts a +3-trial cookie-banner post above a +25-trial docs move, which breaks the owner's main ordering request; the /vs-google top-3 jump is also optimistic.
to10: Reorder strictly by expected trial impact, make the Month 3 competitor pages concrete, and separate ceiling numbers from the plan forecast.

strength: Disciplined ranking by trial impact with honest ranges, strong reasoning about the blog decline, and Monday-ready week-one tasks plus usable titles and meta.
mistake: It leaves the high-CTR docs pages alone instead of adding a trial path, and it lacks a dedicated agency or GA4-migration page for Tomas and Maya's biggest blockers.
to10: Add the docs-to-trial move, add one owned page for the agency/GA4-migration blockers, and name the Month 3 pages rather than leaving them to rules.

strength: Picks recruiting with the paid-seat math and builds the page around Priya's email-tennis pain, round robin, routing forms and security proof in the right order.
mistake: Calls Version A the 'control' even though the current hero is not that copy; it should be framed as one of two new challengers, and a few proof assets still need collecting.
to10: Fix the A/B control naming, supply exact proof-safe security links/language, and replace the proof-to-collect placeholders with real approved assets or a clear collection plan.

strength: Strong segment math and a clean page structure, with a thoughtful final metric that connects hero testing to qualified recruiting-team starts.
mistake: Uses 'Get started' buttons on a team recruiting page and claims text reminders without a source, which breaks the brief's CTA and claim rules.
to10: Change team CTAs to 'Book a demo', remove or bracket unsupported claims like text reminders, add a distinct 'how candidates book' section before features, and give the test a simple sample-size/stop rule.

strength: Best range of asks and the sharpest explanation of the AI-builder margin problem, including direct-vs-partner conversion and burn drivers.
mistake: Too dense for a phone read and it leaves internal drafting language in the body and footer, like 'Ask 2 helps', assumption notes, and the proposed New York base.
to10: Cut it to a tighter phone read, simplify the margin math sentence, and turn the internal confirmations into clean send-ready copy.

strength: Very send-ready: bad news is in the first screen, the table includes runway, and the asks are dated, profiled and one is forwardable.
mistake: The Customer A remedy is thin and the internal assumptions footer would have to come off; it also does not give an expected saving from the 48-hour pause.
to10: Add a simple expected effect from the 48-hour pause and a clearer Customer A learning ask, then remove the assumptions footer.

strength: It picks the winning segment and moment, then turns the pilot into concrete send timing, list rules, exclusions and a usable four-step sequence.
mistake: It projects 8-10% by stacking a segment and trigger the pilot never tested together, and it uses the 9-to-4 proof in step 1 rather than holding it for a later step.
to10: Anchor the expected rate to the observed 6.8-7.9% band unless the team tests the combination, move the proof sentence out of step 1, and keep every email to one unmistakable question and one ask.

strength: It reads like a real peer-to-peer finance email, keeps the right segment and pricing-change trigger, and handles the audit timing objection well.
mistake: Steps 1-3 break the one-question/one-ask rule with extra conditional reply requests, and the 'about 4,100 stay out' count is inconsistent with loading only flagged targets.
to10: Cut each email to one ask, remove unbuilt assets like the one-page summary, fix the list math, and state the expected rate as 6.8-7.9% until a combined segment-plus-trigger test exists.

strength: Complete, runnable hiring kit: the time-zone coverage, a real customer-reply exercise, a weighted scorecard with concrete 1/3/5 anchors, and a credible reviewer-hours plan all fit together.
mistake: The $82,000 salary is buried below the hard parts and job description rather than sitting immediately under the title.
to10: Move the salary to the top of the post, keep the hard parts right behind it, and add a quick line showing how the Priya exercise maps to the scorecard rows.

strength: The post opens correctly with salary and a candid, human explanation of the overnight gap; the application plan and reviewer-hour math are very practical.
mistake: It refers to a longer written exercise and a handoff note but never writes that exercise, so the hiring team still has to invent a key stage; the 100-word 'why this job' also edges back toward a cover letter.
to10: Add the actual shortlist exercise prompt and handoff task, remove the 'why this job' question, and tie the scorecard anchors to those concrete tasks.

strength: Strong retention math, creator/author focus, a strict zero-loss migration gate, and copy that sounds like Raycast and names extension authors.
mistake: It emails all 420,000 existing users on launch day while the update is staged to 10% then 30%, so most recipients cannot yet 'check for updates' and the support risk is underplayed.
to10: Tie the existing-user email to the staged waves, add a concrete support rota and success measures, and remove placeholders so it is publish-ready.

strength: Operational rollout: three waves tied to migration-ticket thresholds, support cover, a day-4 plan B, and correct channel-retention math.
mistake: The migration gate allows 95% carry-over and falls back to a help article for failures, which is too loose for 'don't break my hotkeys'; the email also does not name any extension authors.
to10: Make zero lost hotkeys/settings the gate for existing users and add named author credits to the existing-user email.

strength: Every email is tied to one habit from the retention table, with its own goal and measure, and the drop list explains each cut with the actual numbers (1.4% unsubscribes on the team invite, 0.3% mobile clicks on shortcuts).
